Those glazes can still be seen on tiles in buildings such as the Detroit Public Library and the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington, DC. Designated a National Historic Landmark in 1991, Pewabic continues to operate today as a nonprofit educational institution that offers ceramics classes, holds exhibitions, and sells pottery made on site.

To compare the contributions that Pewabic Pottery’s two founders made to the studio’s early success
To describe the methods Pewabic Pottery uses today to teach ceramics to students
To trace the history of a ceramics studio from its founding to the present day

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from D. H. Lawrence’s 1911 novel The White Peacock, which opens with the narrator standing beside a pond near an old mill.

I stood watching the shadowy fish slide through the gloom of the mill-pond. <u>The whole place was gathered in the musing of old age.</u> The thick-piled trees on the far shore were too dark and sober to dally with the sun; the weeds stood crowded and motionless. Not even a little wind flickered the willows of the islets. The water lay softly, intensely still. Only the thin stream falling through the mill-race murmured to itself of the tumult of life which had once quickened the valley.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It elaborates on the previous sentence’s description of the fish in the pond.
It introduces an impression of the setting that the details in the following sentences develop.
It explains why the narrator has come to the mill-pond on this particular day.
It contrasts the stillness of the pond with the activity in the valley described later in the text.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence says that the whole place seemed lost in “the musing of old age,” an impression of quiet and age. The sentences that follow develop it: the trees are “too dark and sober to dally with the sun,” the weeds are “motionless,” “not even a little wind” stirs the willows, and the water lies “intensely still.” The underlined sentence therefore introduces an impression of the setting that the following details develop.

A.recipe: REL: wrong pointer (previous sentence) and wrong subject (the fish)
A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes “the whole place,” not the fish, and the details that bear it out come in the sentences after it.

C.recipe: INV: a purpose for the narrator’s visit the text never gives
C.why_wrong: The text never says why the narrator is at the pond; it only describes what he sees there.

D.recipe: PART plus REV: the past “tumult of life” misread as present activity
D.why_wrong: The last sentence mentions the “tumult of life which had once quickened the valley,” activity in the past; the text describes no present activity to contrast with the pond, and the underlined sentence makes no comparison.

sources.what: D. H. Lawrence, The White Peacock (1911), Part I, chapter I, opening paragraph; text copied from Project Gutenberg #38561, one sentence left out (the fish as descendants of those that darted from the monks), hence “adapted”

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1911). Key B. Medium F_setup modelled on 2.13 (Melville: the underlined sentence sets up the description that follows). Literary chosen to keep the medium tier’s literary share near CB’s (2.13 is literary). The second sentence of the original (the fish as descendants) is cut so the previous-sentence pointer in A is plainly wrong. Distractors: A REL, C INV, D PART plus REV (compare and contrast are never keyed).

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Dorothy Richardson’s 1915 novel Pointed Roofs, whose central character, Miriam, has recently finished school and is about to leave her family’s home to teach at a school in Germany.

That summer, which still seemed near to her, was going to fade and desert her, leaving nothing behind. <u>To-morrow it would belong to a world which would go on without her, taking no heed.</u> There would still be blissful days. But she would not be in them.

There would be no more silent sunny mornings with all the day ahead and nothing to do and no end anywhere to anything.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals Miriam’s relief that she will soon escape the familiar routines of her family’s crowded household.
It suggests that Miriam expects the coming summer to be less pleasant than the one just past.
It conveys Miriam’s sense that the life she has enjoyed will carry on without her once she leaves.
It indicates that Miriam has already begun to forget what happened during the previous summer.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence says that the summer Miriam loved “would belong to a world which would go on without her, taking no heed.” The sentences around it reinforce this feeling: “There would still be blissful days. But she would not be in them,” and there would be “no more silent sunny mornings” for her. The sentence thus conveys Miriam’s sense that the life she has enjoyed will carry on without her once she leaves.

A.recipe: REV: sorrow at leaving read as relief
A.why_wrong: The text dwells on what Miriam will lose, such as “silent sunny mornings,” and shows no relief at going away.

B.recipe: LIT plus REV: the summer read literally and its quality reversed
B.why_wrong: The text says “there would still be blissful days”; the loss is that Miriam will not be there to enjoy them, not that they will be less pleasant.

D.recipe: REV: the summer “still seemed near to her”
D.why_wrong: The text says the summer “still seemed near to her”; Miriam fears it will fade once she leaves, not that she has already forgotten it.

sources.what: Dorothy Richardson, Pointed Roofs (1915), chapter I, section 1, Miriam’s last evening at home before leaving to teach in Germany; text copied from Project Gutenberg #3019, ending at the first clause of the next sentence (its semicolon made a period), hence “adapted”

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1915, public domain in the US). Key C. Medium F_lit modelled on 2.23 (Woolf: what a figurative span emphasizes about a character’s state). Richardson appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: A REV (the relief Miriam feels later in the chapter is outside the excerpt), B LIT plus REV, D REV.

items.passage: Estimating how much sea level has risen since the nineteenth century requires long-term measurements, but such records are scarce in the Southern Hemisphere. John Hunter and colleagues addressed this shortage by turning to an unusual historical source at Port Arthur, Tasmania, where in 1841 Thomas Lempriere and the explorer James Clark Ross carved a sea-level benchmark into a rock face on the small Isle of the Dead. Comparing Lempriere’s tide measurements from 1841 and 1842, referenced to that benchmark, with observations made between 1999 and 2002, the researchers estimated that local sea level had risen by approximately 0.8 millimeters per year since 1841.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It explains why sea level has risen faster in the Southern Hemisphere than elsewhere, then describes a study that confirmed this pattern.
It describes a set of historical tide measurements, then explains why researchers concluded that the measurements were too unreliable to use.
It summarizes a dispute among researchers about the rate of sea-level rise, then presents evidence supporting one side of that dispute.
It notes a shortage of data that limits research on a particular question, then describes how one team of researchers worked around it.
items.explanation: The text first notes a problem: estimating sea-level rise “requires long-term measurements, but such records are scarce in the Southern Hemisphere.” It then describes how Hunter and colleagues “addressed this shortage by turning to an unusual historical source,” comparing Lempriere’s tide measurements from 1841 and 1842, referenced to a benchmark carved into rock, with modern observations. The text therefore notes a shortage of data and then describes how a team of researchers worked around it.

A.recipe: wholly wrong template: invented comparison and confirmation
A.why_wrong: The text says long records are scarce in the Southern Hemisphere, not that sea level has risen faster there, and it compares no regions.

B.recipe: first move partly right, second move reversed
B.why_wrong: The researchers used Lempriere’s measurements to estimate the rise in sea level; the text never says they found the measurements unreliable.

C.recipe: wholly wrong template: a debate and one side’s evidence
C.why_wrong: The text describes no disagreement among researchers; it describes a shortage of data and a way of working around it.

sources.what: Research Data Australia, Historical observations of sea level at Port Arthur, Tasmania: Lempriere’s tide observations (1837 to at least 1842, digitised 1840 to 1842); a sea-level benchmark struck on a small cliff on the Isle of the Dead by T. J. Lempriere and Captain James Clark Ross in 1841; purpose: past sea-level rise in the Southern Hemisphere; paper Hunter, Coleman and Pugh 2003, Geophysical Research Letters 30(7)

Hunter, Coleman, Pugh 2003 abstract (EarthRef): records from 1841 to 1842 and 1999 to 2002 give a sea-level rise relative to the land of about 0.8 mm per year from 1841 to 2002; the result matters for the Southern Hemisphere, “where there is a dearth of other such data”

items.notes: Area: natural science (oceanography, climate history). Key D. Medium S7 modelled on 2.16 (problem in research, then a researcher’s approach). Key wording avoids 2.16’s key. Distractors: two wholly wrong templates (A, C) and one with the first move partly right and the second reversed (B), as in medium structure items.

items.passage:
The following text is from “The Serving Girl,” a poem by Gladys May Casely Hayford, a writer born in what is now Ghana. The poem was published in the 1927 anthology Caroling Dusk.

The calabash wherein she served my food,
Was smooth and polished as sandalwood:
Fish, as white as the foam of the sea,
Peppered, and golden fried for me.
She brought palm wine that carelessly slips
From the sleeping palm tree’s honeyed lips.
<u>But who can guess, or even surmise
The countless things she served with her eyes?</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined lines in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that the girl offered the speaker something more than the meal she brought.
It reveals that the speaker could not tell what kinds of food the girl had prepared.
It indicates that the girl was unhappy about having to wait on the speaker.
It emphasizes how many separate dishes the girl served during the meal.
items.explanation: The first six lines list the food and drink the girl brings: fish “golden fried for me” and “palm wine.” The underlined lines then turn, with “But,” to “the countless things she served with her eyes,” which no one “can guess, or even surmise.” Since these things are served with her eyes rather than in a dish, the lines suggest that the girl offered the speaker something more than the meal itself.

B.recipe: LIT: “who can guess” read as confusion about the food
B.why_wrong: The speaker names the food clearly, fish and palm wine; what cannot be guessed is what the girl served “with her eyes,” not the meal.

C.recipe: INV: an unhappy feeling the poem never gives the girl
C.why_wrong: Nothing in the poem suggests the girl is unhappy; the speaker describes her serving warmly, with no complaint from her.

D.recipe: LIT: “countless things she served” read as dishes of food
D.why_wrong: The “countless things” are served “with her eyes,” so they are not dishes; the poem mentions only fish and palm wine.

sources.what: Gladys May Casely Hayford, “The Serving Girl,” in Caroling Dusk: An Anthology of Verse by Negro Poets, ed. Countee Cullen (1927), whole poem copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #76889; her own note there says she was born at Axim on the Gold Coast in 1904

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, 1927, public domain in the US). Key A. Easy F_lit modelled on 1.23 (underlined lines of a short poem, what they convey) and 1.1. Source line follows the bank’s Caroling Dusk precedent (w3b3_15) since the poem’s first periodical publication is not confirmed. Casely Hayford appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: B and D literalize the closing image, C invents a feeling. Options start “It” like 1.23’s.

fixes: option A “the meal she brought him” made “the meal she brought”: the poem never gives the speaker’s sex

items.passage:
The following text is from Carl Ewald’s book My Little Boy, translated from the Danish by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos in 1906. The narrator is describing his young son.

He has a habit which I love.

When we are walking together and there is anything that impresses him, he lets go my hand for a moment. <u>Then, when he has investigated the phenomenon and arrived at a result, I feel his little fist in mine again.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows that the boy is afraid to explore anything new unless his father is beside him.
It shows how the boy returns to his father after briefly exploring something on his own.
It explains why the narrator worries whenever his son lets go of his hand on their walks.
It suggests that the boy is becoming more independent than his father would like him to be.
items.explanation: The narrator describes “a habit which I love”: when something impresses his son, the boy “lets go my hand for a moment.” The underlined sentence completes the habit: once the boy “has investigated the phenomenon and arrived at a result,” the narrator feels “his little fist in mine again.” The sentence therefore shows how the boy returns to his father after briefly exploring something on his own.

A.recipe: REV: the boy explores on his own
A.why_wrong: The boy lets go of his father’s hand to investigate whatever impresses him, so he is not afraid to explore without his father beside him.

C.recipe: REV: the narrator loves the habit
C.why_wrong: The narrator calls this “a habit which I love”; he does not say he worries when his son lets go.

D.recipe: INV: a parental worry about independence the text never states
D.why_wrong: The boy lets go only “for a moment” and then takes his father’s hand again, and the narrator expresses no wish that the boy were less independent.

sources.what: Carl Ewald, My Little Boy, translated from the Danish by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos (Scribner’s, copyright 1906), section I; text copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #35543 (the Danish original’s year is not confirmed, so the source line gives only the translation’s)

items.notes: Area: literature (book of sketches, translated, 1906). Key B. Easy F_lit modelled on 1.20 (Erdrich: a sentence offering a detail that shows a trait) and 1.1. Ewald appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: A and C reversals, D an invented worry.

items.passage:
The following text is from Helene Johnson’s poem “What Do I Care for Morning,” published in the 1927 anthology Caroling Dusk.

What do I care for morning,
For a shivering aspen tree,
For sun flowers and sumac
Opening greedily?
What do I care for morning,
For the glare of the rising sun,
For a sparrow’s noisy prating,
For another day begun?
Give me the beauty of evening,
The cool consummation of night,
And the moon like a love-sick lady,
Listless and wan and white.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the changes the speaker notices as morning gradually turns into night
To explain why the speaker has trouble sleeping through the night
To express the speaker’s preference for evening over morning
To celebrate the beauty of the plants and birds that appear at dawn
items.explanation: The speaker twice asks, “What do I care for morning,” dismissing its “glare” and “noisy prating.” The speaker then asks instead for “the beauty of evening” and “the cool consummation of night.” The text therefore expresses the speaker’s preference for evening over morning.

A.recipe: INV: a gradual change over a day the poem never traces
A.why_wrong: The poem sets morning and evening against each other; it never describes the hours in which one turns into the other.

B.recipe: INV: a problem with sleep the poem never mentions
B.why_wrong: Nothing in the poem refers to the speaker’s sleep; the speaker simply prefers evening and night to morning.

D.recipe: REV: the morning scenes are dismissed, not praised
D.why_wrong: The speaker mentions plants and a sparrow only to ask “What do I care for morning”; the beauty the speaker wants is that of evening.

sources.what: Helene Johnson, “What Do I Care for Morning,” in Caroling Dusk (1927), lines 1 to 12 of 28, copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #76889

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, 1927, public domain in the US). Key C, the shortest option, as easy purpose keys often are. Lines 1 to 12 end at the first full stop after the turn to evening. Johnson appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: A and B INV, D REV.

fixes: explanation and D’s why_wrong say “the speaker” instead of “she”: the poem never gives the speaker’s sex

items.passage: In 1944, Brazilian artist and activist Abdias do Nascimento founded the Teatro Experimental do Negro (Black Experimental Theater) in Rio de Janeiro. Nascimento had resolved to establish a Black theater company to combat racism after attending a production in Peru in which a white actor wore makeup to portray a Black character. The company’s inaugural production, presented in 1945, was Eugene O’Neill’s play The Emperor Jones. The company later assembled the performers for Orfeu da Conceição, a play subsequently adapted into the internationally acclaimed film Black Orpheus.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why the Teatro Experimental do Negro chose to perform plays by American writers
To compare the theater of Brazil with the theater of Peru during the 1940s
To argue that Black Orpheus is the most important work connected with Nascimento
To describe the origins and some achievements of a Brazilian theater company
items.explanation: The text explains how and why Nascimento founded the Teatro Experimental do Negro “to combat racism,” then names two of its achievements: its “inaugural production,” The Emperor Jones, and the performers it assembled for Orfeu da Conceição, which became the film Black Orpheus. The text therefore describes the origins and some achievements of a Brazilian theater company.

A.recipe: BROAD plus INV: one play by O’Neill turned into a policy and a motive
A.why_wrong: The text mentions only one play by an American writer and gives no reason for choosing it.

B.recipe: INV: a comparison the text never makes
B.why_wrong: Peru appears only as the place where Nascimento saw one production; the text does not compare the theater of the two countries.

C.recipe: STANCE plus BROAD: an argument about ranking
C.why_wrong: The text simply notes that the company assembled the performers for the play that became Black Orpheus; it never ranks that work above others.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Abdias do Nascimento: in Lima, Peru, he saw The Emperor Jones performed by a white actor in blackface and decided to create a Black theater in Brazil to fight racism; founded the Teatro Experimental do Negro (TEN) in 1944 in Rio de Janeiro; TEN premiered on May 8, 1945, with O’Neill’s The Emperor Jones; TEN organized the cast for Orfeu da Conceição, later adapted into the film Black Orpheus

items.notes: Area: humanities (theater, Afro-Brazilian history). Key D, the shortest option. Easy P_profile modelled on 1.4, 1.6 and 1.10. Details the source does not state (literacy classes, the Quilombo newspaper, the cast of the 1945 production) are left out. Distractors: A BROAD plus INV, B INV (compare is never keyed), C STANCE.

fixes: checked neighbor, kept: live text_structure_and_purpose.P_profile.easy.w3b3_19 (Victoria Santa Cruz, Cumanana, Peru’s first Black theater company) is a person profile in another country with different facts; not a clone

items.passage: Ships that are no longer needed are sometimes deliberately sunk to create artificial reefs, providing fish and other marine organisms with a durable surface for shelter and feeding. <u>One example is the decommissioned aircraft carrier USS Oriskany, which was sunk in the Gulf of Mexico in 2006, approximately 24 miles off the coast of Pensacola, Florida.</u> Before the sinking, many hazardous substances were removed from the vessel. Its flight deck now rests more than 130 feet below the surface, and the wreck has become a popular destination for recreational divers.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why the US Navy stopped using the USS Oriskany as an aircraft carrier.
It provides an example of the practice described in the previous sentence.
It describes the hazardous substances that were removed from the ship before it was sunk.
It argues that the USS Oriskany is the most popular diving site in the Gulf of Mexico.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general statement: ships “are sometimes deliberately sunk to create artificial reefs.” The underlined sentence then names “one example,” the USS Oriskany, “which was sunk in the Gulf of Mexico in 2006.” The underlined sentence thus provides an example of the practice described in the previous sentence.

A.recipe: LIT plus INV: “decommissioned” turned into an explanation
A.why_wrong: The sentence calls the ship “decommissioned” but never explains why the navy stopped using it.

C.recipe: PART: the content of the following sentence
C.why_wrong: The removal of “many hazardous substances” is mentioned in the sentence after the underlined one, and the text never says what those substances were.

D.recipe: STANCE plus INV: a ranking the text never makes
D.why_wrong: The text says only that the wreck “has become a popular destination for recreational divers”; it never compares it with other diving sites.

sources.what: Wikipedia, USS Oriskany: sunk on 17 May 2006 as an artificial reef in 210 ft of water in the Gulf of Mexico, about 24 mi south of Pensacola; environmental review and remediation removed toxic substances first; flight deck about 135 ft down (about 145 ft after Hurricane Gustav, 2008); accessible to recreational divers and rated one of the top wreck-diving sites

items.notes: Area: natural science and history (artificial reefs, a naval ship). Key B. Easy F_example modelled on 1.3 (a sentence giving one example of a general statement in the previous sentence) and 1.14. Reviewer replacement for the Promenade plantée item, a concept clone of live transitions.X1_example.easy.w1b2_17 (railway lines turned into parks, same example frame) and of the round-1 High Line item. No “largest vessel ever sunk as a reef” claim, since the SS United States is planned to take that record; no claim about fish on the wreck, which the source barely covers. Distractors: A LIT plus INV, C PART (next sentence), D STANCE.

fixes: replaced: the Promenade plantée item cloned live transitions.X1_example.easy.w1b2_17 (“cities have transformed obsolete elevated highways and railway lines into public parks”, same example frame) and named the round-1 High Line; new subject USS Oriskany sunk as an artificial reef (Wikipedia), claimed in claims.txt, key letter B kept

items.passage: In 2015, ecologist Thomas Crowther and colleagues estimated that Earth holds roughly 3 trillion trees. That number is more than seven times the previous figure of about 400 billion. <u>The earlier figure had been calculated from satellite images and estimates of forest area, without any information gathered on the ground.</u> Crowther’s team instead compiled tree counts from more than 400,000 forest plots worldwide. The researchers then combined those counts with satellite data to map how densely trees grow in each region.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It presents the main finding of the study discussed in the text.
It explains why the number of trees growing on Earth has steadily declined over the past several centuries.
It describes a shortcoming of an earlier estimate of the number of trees on Earth.
It summarizes a criticism that other researchers made of Crowther’s methods.
items.explanation: The text reports Crowther and colleagues’ estimate of “roughly 3 trillion trees,” far more than “the previous figure of about 400 billion.” The underlined sentence explains that the earlier figure was calculated “without any information gathered on the ground,” and the next sentences show how Crowther’s team avoided that problem by using “tree counts from more than 400,000 forest plots.” The underlined sentence therefore describes a shortcoming of an earlier estimate.

A.recipe: REL: the main finding is in the previous sentence
A.why_wrong: The study’s main finding, about 3 trillion trees, appears in the first sentence; the underlined sentence concerns how the earlier figure was calculated.

B.recipe: INV: a decline the text never mentions
B.why_wrong: The text compares two estimates of how many trees exist; it says nothing about the number of trees changing over time.

D.recipe: SWAP: the limitation moved from the old estimate to Crowther’s study
D.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes a weakness of the earlier figure, not a criticism of Crowther’s methods, which the last sentence presents as an improvement.

sources.what: Yale School of the Environment news (2015): the previous estimate of just over 400 billion trees was generated using satellite imagery and estimates of forest area but did not incorporate any information from the ground; the new study used data from more than 400,000 forest plots, from national forest inventories and peer-reviewed studies, combined with satellite imagery; more than 3 trillion trees, about seven and a half times previous estimates
Crowther et al. 2015, Nature 525: 201-205, Mapping tree density at a global scale: about 3.04 trillion trees, an order of magnitude higher than the previous estimate

items.notes: Area: natural science (forest ecology). Key C. Easy F_limit modelled on 1.16. To avoid 1.16’s skeleton (two competing views, “However, many ... relied on incomplete data sets,” then a large new data set and agreement), the passage opens with the new result, then the old figure’s limitation, then the new method; no competing views, no signal word. Distractors: A REL (previous sentence’s job), B INV, D SWAP.

items.passage: <u>Until 2017, the earliest chemical evidence of grape wine in the Near East came from Hajji Firuz Tepe, a village site in Iran’s Zagros Mountains dating to about 5400–5000 BCE.</u> That year, Patrick McGovern and colleagues reported wine residues absorbed into pottery from two Neolithic settlements in Georgia, in the South Caucasus. The vessels had been manufactured around 6000–5800 BCE. These enormous jars, among the earliest pottery produced in the region, probably served as containers for fermenting, aging, and serving wine.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It identifies the older record that the discovery described in the following sentence went on to surpass.
It explains how researchers were able to detect traces of wine in ancient pottery.
It describes an earlier discovery that the researchers working in Georgia later demonstrated had been dated incorrectly.
It presents the main conclusion that the rest of the text supports with several examples.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence says that, “until 2017,” the earliest chemical evidence of grape wine in the Near East came from Hajji Firuz Tepe, dating to “about 5400–5000 BCE.” The next sentences report wine residues in Georgian pottery “manufactured around 6000–5800 BCE,” which is older. The underlined sentence therefore identifies the earlier record that the Georgian discovery surpassed, helping show why that discovery matters.

B.recipe: INV: a method the text never describes
B.why_wrong: The text says wine residues were found “absorbed into pottery” but never explains how they were detected, and the underlined sentence concerns an earlier find.

C.recipe: REV plus INV: an older record treated as a dating error
C.why_wrong: The Georgian finds are older than the Iranian ones, but the text never says the Iranian evidence was misdated; it was simply the earliest known until 2017.

D.recipe: REL: wrong role (main claim with examples)
D.why_wrong: The underlined sentence gives background about an earlier find; the rest of the text describes one new discovery, not several examples supporting a conclusion.

sources.what: McGovern et al. 2017, PNAS 114(48): E10309-E10318, Early Neolithic wine of Georgia in the South Caucasus: residues absorbed into pottery from Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora give the earliest biomolecular evidence of grape wine in the Near East, about 6000 to 5800 BC; previously the earliest was Hajji Firuz Tepe, northwestern Zagros Mountains, Iran, about 5400 to 5000 BC; the very large jars, among the earliest pottery in the Near East, probably served for fermentation, aging and serving

items.notes: Area: history (archaeology of food and drink). Key A. Easy F_setup modelled on 1.2 (context that clarifies the significance of a finding). To avoid 1.2’s skeleton (finding first, then “Before the discovery, X was thought ...”, “but the discovery suggests”), the underlined context sentence comes first, there is no “before/but” turn, and the key’s wording differs from 1.2’s. “In the Near East” keeps the claim as narrow as the source.

items.passage: Recursion, the embedding of a structure within another structure of the same type, is frequently regarded as a foundation of human linguistic competence. To determine whether other animals might possess the capacity, Diana Liao, Andreas Nieder, and colleagues adapted a protocol previously administered to humans and monkeys: carrion crows learned to peck sequences of paired symbols, such as brackets, and were then tested on unfamiliar pairings. The crows generated center-embedded sequences about as reliably as young children do, outperforming macaques, which suggests that the capacity is not exclusive to primates.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It summarizes research that asked whether a capacity observed in crows also appears in primates and reports that young children share the capacity but monkeys lack it.
It summarizes a study that gave crows a task first used with primates and reports results suggesting that a capacity linked to human language exists beyond primates.
It describes how a test developed for primates was adapted for crows and explains that the crows succeeded only after the sequences were made shorter than those given to children.
It describes how crows performed on a test first designed for primates and suggests that the birds can understand human language about as well as young children can.
items.explanation: The text describes recursion as “frequently regarded as a foundation of human linguistic competence.” It then reports that Liao, Nieder, and colleagues “adapted a protocol previously administered to humans and monkeys” for carrion crows, which performed “about as reliably as young children do, outperforming macaques, which suggests that the capacity is not exclusive to primates.” Choice B names both parts: the borrowed test and what its result suggests.

A.recipe: right elements, direction of the test reversed and a result invented (SWAP)
A.why_wrong: The study ran the other way: the researchers “adapted a protocol previously administered to humans and monkeys” to see whether crows share a capacity tied to human language. The text also never says monkeys lack the capacity; it says only that the crows outperformed macaques.

C.recipe: first clause true, later clause invents a condition (INV)
C.why_wrong: The test was adapted for crows, but the text never says the sequences were shortened or that the crows succeeded only under easier conditions; they were “tested on unfamiliar pairings.”

D.recipe: first clause true, later clause overreaches (BROAD)
D.why_wrong: The crows did take a test first given to primates, but the text claims only that they handled center-embedded sequences “about as reliably as young children do.” Recursion is called “a foundation of human linguistic competence,” not the whole of it, so the result says nothing about understanding human language.

sources.what: Liao, Brecht, Johnston, Nieder 2022, Science Advances (PubMed abstract): recursion often considered uniquely human; protocol adopted from a study of humans and nonhuman primates; crows tested on center-embedded structure with never-before-seen bracket pairings perform on par with children and outperform macaques; recursive capabilities not limited to the primate genealogy

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal cognition). Key B. Key parts: 2 (a test borrowed from primate studies was given to crows; the result suggests the capacity is not limited to primates). Section 6 checks: key 29 words; options 27 to 30 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: C and D (2 of 3); A keeps the elements and reverses the test's direction. The source says the crows perform on par with children; the passage softens it to “about as reliably.”
band7_moves: dual, hedged purpose: the key joins the study's borrowed method with what its result suggests (“suggesting ... not limited to primates”)
abstract key: “a capacity linked to human language” replaces recursion, brackets and center-embedding, and “exists beyond primates” paraphrases “not exclusive to primates”
C and D open with a true account of the study and fail in a later clause (an invented condition, an overreach from recursion to language); A reverses which animal the borrowed test was meant for

The following text is adapted from Thomas Chandler Haliburton’s 1836 novel The Clockmaker. Sam Slick, a clock peddler, has just left a clock with Deacon Flint and his wife, saying he will collect it later.

“That,” said the Clockmaker as soon as we were mounted, “that I call ‘human natur’!’ Now that clock is sold for forty dollars—it cost me just six dollars and fifty cents. Mrs. Flint will never let Mrs. Steel [a neighbor] have the refusal [first chance to buy it]—nor will the deacon learn until I call for the clock, that having once indulged in the use of a superfluity, how difficult it is to give it up.”
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes a character’s plan to sell a clock to a neighbor of the family with whom he has left it.
It reveals a character’s regret at having asked a respected family to pay far more for a clock than it cost him.
It describes a character’s belief that people come to value a luxury less once they have grown used to owning it.
It presents a character’s explanation of why an apparent favor to a family will in fact secure a sale.
items.explanation: Slick has only left the clock with the Flints, yet he says, “Now that clock is sold for forty dollars.” He then gives his reason: the deacon will learn “that having once indulged in the use of a superfluity, how difficult it is to give it up.” The text therefore presents his explanation of why leaving the clock, which looks like a favor, will make the sale, as choice D says.

A.recipe: a named minor figure taken as the buyer (SWAP)
A.why_wrong: Mrs. Steel is mentioned, but Slick says “Mrs. Flint will never let Mrs. Steel [a neighbor] have the refusal.” He expects the Flints themselves to keep the clock, which is why he says “that clock is sold.”

B.recipe: true contrast in prices, wrong feeling (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: Slick does contrast the price, “forty dollars,” with what the clock “cost me,” but he shows no regret. He calls the arrangement “human natur’” with evident satisfaction.

C.why_wrong: Slick says the opposite: “having once indulged in the use of a superfluity,” a person finds it “difficult ... to give it up.” Owning a luxury makes it harder, not easier, to do without.

sources.what: Haliburton, The Clockmaker; or, The Sayings and Doings of Samuel Slick, of Slickville, No. II “The Clockmaker,” checked against Gutenberg 9196: the opening of the closing speech to the narrator after the clock is left at Deacon Flint’s; small capitals of HUMAN NATUR’ set in lower case, “--” set as closed dashes, two bracketed glosses added; the speech is cut after “to give it up.” The Clockmaker first appeared in the Novascotian and was published as a book in 1836 (Wikipedia, Haliburton bibliography)

items.passage: For decades, scholars commonly maintained that people in ancient Greece and Rome almost invariably read aloud and that silent reading was so exceptional that it astonished anyone who witnessed it. <u>In his Confessions, composed around 400 CE, Augustine recalls his puzzlement at observing the bishop Ambrose read with his eyes moving across the page while his voice remained silent.</u> In a 1968 article, however, classicist Bernard Knox contends that this conventional view goes too far: he identifies scenes in plays performed in fifth-century BCE Athens in which characters read letters and oracles silently, as though the practice were entirely unremarkable.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes an instance that seems to confirm a long-standing scholarly view of ancient reading, a view that, according to the text, Knox considers exaggerated.
It presents a case that appears to bear out a widely held view of ancient reading, a view that Knox, according to the text, supports with evidence from Athenian plays.
It identifies the earliest surviving description of silent reading, which, according to the text, Knox shows to be less trustworthy than other scholars had assumed.
It offers an example consistent with a long-standing view of ancient reading, a view that Knox, according to the text, accepts for fifth-century Athens but rejects for Augustine’s era.
items.explanation: The first sentence reports that scholars commonly maintained that “silent reading was so exceptional that it astonished anyone who witnessed it.” The underlined sentence gives a case that fits that view: Augustine “recalls his puzzlement at observing the bishop Ambrose read with his eyes moving across the page while his voice remained silent.” The last sentence then says that Knox “contends that this conventional view goes too far.” So the underlined sentence describes an instance that seems to confirm a long-standing view that, according to the text, Knox considers exaggerated, as choice A says.

B.recipe: first clause true, Knox’s stance flipped (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: Augustine’s account does fit the scholars’ view, but Knox does not support that view. He “contends that this conventional view goes too far,” and he cites the Athenian plays against it: in them, characters read “silently, as though the practice were entirely unremarkable.”

C.why_wrong: The text never calls Augustine’s account the earliest description of silent reading; it mentions plays from “fifth-century BCE Athens,” centuries earlier. Nor does it say Knox questions whether Augustine’s account can be trusted; he disputes the broader view.

D.recipe: first clause true, Knox’s position reversed by period (REV)
D.why_wrong: Knox does not accept the view for fifth-century Athens. His evidence comes from “plays performed in fifth-century BCE Athens,” in which characters read letters and oracles silently, so he uses that period to argue against the view; the text reports no opinion of his about Augustine’s era.

sources.what: Bernard M. W. Knox, “Silent Reading in Antiquity,” Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies 9 (1968) 421-435 (scan, fetched and read): since Balogh’s 1927 article it had become standard doctrine that silent reading was so rare that it aroused astonishment; Augustine on Ambrose is the main exhibit; Knox finds that this goes too far and cites Euripides’ Hippolytus (Theseus reads Phaedra’s letter silently) and Aristophanes’ Knights (an oracle read silently) to show that silent reading of letters and oracles was taken for granted in fifth- and fourth-century Athens, while granting that literary texts were normally read aloud

items.passage: Tarabai Shinde’s Stri Purush Tulana (A Comparison Between Women and Men), a Marathi pamphlet printed in Pune in 1882, was prompted by a newspaper article about the prosecution of a young widow. Yet Shinde went well beyond the case itself. Whereas most reformers of the period concentrated on particular hardships endured by widows, she examined the assumptions about women built into the society around her, implying that women everywhere were similarly oppressed. The pamphlet’s hostile reception discouraged her from publishing again, and it remained largely unknown until it was rediscovered and republished in 1975.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why reformers in nineteenth-century Pune rejected an essay that confined itself to the hardships faced by widows
To argue that a Marathi pamphlet deserves greater recognition than it has received even since its republication in 1975
To describe an 1882 pamphlet whose critique reached further than those of its contemporaries and to note its long obscurity
To show how an 1882 pamphlet led reformers to turn their attention from the hardships of widows to the condition of women generally
items.explanation: The text says that Shinde “went well beyond the case itself”: “Whereas most reformers of the period concentrated on particular hardships endured by widows, she examined the assumptions about women built into the society around her.” It then notes that the pamphlet “remained largely unknown until it was rediscovered and republished in 1975.” The text thus describes a pamphlet whose critique went further than others of its time and notes how long it was overlooked, as choice C says.

A.recipe: reversal of the pamphlet's scope, invented rejection by reformers (REV)
A.why_wrong: The text says Shinde did not confine herself to widows’ hardships; she “went well beyond the case itself.” It mentions a “hostile reception” but never says reformers rejected the pamphlet or explains a rejection.

B.recipe: neutral profile read as an argument (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: The text reports the pamphlet’s reception and rediscovery without arguing that it deserves more recognition, and it says nothing about how the work has been received since 1975.

D.why_wrong: Shinde did move beyond widows’ hardships, but the text never says she changed other reformers’ focus. On the contrary, the pamphlet “remained largely unknown” for nearly a century.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Tarabai Shinde: Stri Purush Tulana, published in Marathi in 1882 (Shri Shivaji Press, Pune), written in response to an 1881 Pune Vaibhav article about the criminal case of a young Brahmin widow; Tharu and Lalita: while others focused on the Hindu widow's hardships, Shinde broadened the analysis to the ideological fabric of patriarchal society, implying that women everywhere are similarly oppressed; hostile reception meant she did not publish again; the work remained largely unknown until it was rediscovered and republished in 1975

items.passage: Despite decades of oil revenue, Nigeria’s economy performed poorly over the long term, an outcome that Xavier Sala-i-Martin and Arvind Subramanian attribute mainly to waste and corruption, which weakened the public institutions on which sustained growth depends. Many other countries rich in oil or minerals have likewise tended to grow more slowly than resource-poor countries. Botswana, however, departs from that pattern: although rich in diamonds, it had the world’s highest rate of per capita growth in the 35 years after its independence, a success that Daron Acemoglu and colleagues trace largely to institutions that protected private property and limited the power of political elites.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes and explains one country’s economic difficulties, notes that similar countries have faced the same difficulties, and then argues that a second country’s policies would solve them.
It reports a finding and the explanation researchers give for it, indicates that the finding fits a wider pattern, and then presents a case that the text suggests casts doubt on that explanation.
It presents a finding about one country, explains why economists considered that finding surprising, and then describes a second country whose experience confirmed it.

It accounts for one country’s experience, indicates that the experience is typical of countries with similar resources, and then describes a country that is an exception and accounts for that exception.
items.explanation: The text first reports that Nigeria’s economy “performed poorly over the long term” and gives Sala-i-Martin and Subramanian’s account of why: “waste and corruption.” It then generalizes: “Many other countries rich in oil or minerals have likewise tended to grow more slowly than resource-poor countries.” Finally it says that Botswana “departs from that pattern” and gives Acemoglu and colleagues’ account of the exception: “institutions that protected private property and limited the power of political elites.” Choice D follows those three moves.

A.recipe: moves 1 and 2 kept, invented recommendation for move 3 (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text does explain Nigeria’s difficulties and say that other resource-rich countries have fared similarly, but it never argues that Botswana’s policies would solve them. It presents Botswana as an exception and explains its success.

B.recipe: moves 1 and 2 kept, move 3 given a stance the text does not take (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: Botswana does not cast doubt on the explanation of Nigeria’s poor performance, which blames weakened “public institutions.” The text credits Botswana’s success to “institutions that protected private property,” so the exception fits that explanation rather than undermining it.

C.recipe: invented surprise and a reversed final move (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text never says economists found Nigeria’s poor performance surprising, and Botswana does not confirm it: Botswana “departs from that pattern,” with “the world’s highest rate of per capita growth.”

sources.what: Sala-i-Martin and Subramanian 2003, Addressing the Natural Resource Curse: An Illustration from Nigeria, NBER Working Paper 9804 (RePEc abstract): oil and minerals hurt growth through their deleterious impact on institutional quality; waste and corruption from oil, rather than Dutch disease, responsible for Nigeria’s poor long-run economic performance

Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson 2002, An African Success Story: Botswana, CEPR Discussion Paper 3219 (RePEc abstract): Botswana had the highest rate of per capita growth of any country in the last 35 years; good policies chosen because institutions of private property were in place; inclusive pre-colonial institutions placed constraints on political elites; diamond rents also helped

Sachs and Warner 1995, Natural Resource Abundance and Economic Growth, NBER Working Paper 5398 (RePEc abstract): economies with abundant natural resources have tended to grow less rapidly than natural-resource-scarce economies, 1971 to 1989

items.passage: Many crocodyliforms that coexisted with dinosaurs possessed teeth unlike those of any living crocodile, with multiple cusps and ridged surfaces, and paleontologists have long suspected that some were herbivorous. <u>Testing that suspicion has been difficult, however, because no living reptile or mammal has teeth closely comparable in shape to theirs.</u> Keegan Melstrom and Randall Irmis therefore quantified dental complexity rather than shape, using a measure known to correspond with diet in living animals. Their analysis indicates that herbivory evolved independently among crocodyliforms at least three times.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It identifies an obstacle to testing a long-standing suspicion, one that the researchers discussed later in the text got around by measuring a different property of the teeth.
It presents a difficulty in testing what paleontologists have long suspected, a difficulty that the text says the researchers overcame by developing a new way to compare tooth shapes.
It explains why paleontologists first suspected that some extinct crocodyliforms ate plants, a suspicion that the text goes on to say the researchers’ measurements contradicted.
It describes a difference between extinct and living animals that, according to the text, led the researchers to conclude that crocodyliforms changed their diets as their teeth evolved.
items.explanation: The first sentence reports a long-standing suspicion that some crocodyliforms “were herbivorous.” The underlined sentence explains why it has been hard to test: “no living reptile or mammal has teeth closely comparable in shape to theirs.” The next sentence says Melstrom and Irmis “therefore quantified dental complexity rather than shape,” and their analysis supports the suspicion. So the underlined sentence identifies an obstacle that the researchers got around by measuring a different property, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The sentence does present a difficulty, and the researchers did overcome it, but not by comparing shapes: because “no living reptile or mammal has teeth closely comparable in shape to theirs,” they “quantified dental complexity rather than shape.”

C.recipe: wrong role for the span, reversed result (REL)
C.why_wrong: The reason for the suspicion is given in the first sentence (the teeth’s “multiple cusps and ridged surfaces”), not the underlined one, and the measurements support the suspicion rather than contradict it.

D.recipe: first clause loosely true, invented conclusion (INV)
D.why_wrong: The sentence does point to a difference from living animals, but the text never says the researchers concluded that diets changed as teeth evolved; it reports that herbivory “evolved independently ... at least three times.”

sources.what: Melstrom and Irmis 2019, Current Biology (PubMed abstract): unusual crocodyliform dental morphologies suggest varied feeding ecologies, but tests are hindered by the lack of directly comparable dental morphologies in living reptiles and mammals; using the orientation patch count rotated method and discrete features, Mesozoic crocodyliforms included likely omnivores and herbivores; high-complexity dentitions developed independently at least three times

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology). Key A. Key parts: 2 (an obstacle to testing; what the later researchers did about it). Span role: a means (a set-up) whose job depends on the sentence after it. items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Angela Brazil’s 1906 novel The Fortunes of Philippa. Philippa, raised in South America, has been sent to live with relatives in England.

I came to England with the swallows, and I think I felt as much a bird of passage as they; more so, indeed, for all the young swallows had been reared under northern skies and were but returning home, while I was as yet a stranger in a new land.

I was so utterly weary with my journey, and I felt so forlornly shy at the sight of so many strange faces around me, that, forgetting both my manners and my good intentions, I burst into a flood of tears, and refused all comfort.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To suggest that the narrator, like the swallows, is returning to a country she knew as a young child
To explain why the narrator’s relatives decided that she should come to live in England
To convey the narrator’s sense of being a stranger as she arrives in an unfamiliar country
To describe the narrator’s efforts to hide her shyness from the relatives who have come to meet her
items.explanation: The narrator says she felt “as much a bird of passage” as the swallows, and “more so,” because they “were but returning home, while I was as yet a stranger in a new land.” She then describes feeling “so forlornly shy at the sight of so many strange faces” that she “burst into a flood of tears.” Both paragraphs convey her sense of being a stranger on arriving in England, as choice C says.

A.recipe: the image read literally and reversed (LIT)
A.why_wrong: The narrator contrasts herself with the swallows: they “were but returning home,” while she “was as yet a stranger in a new land.” Nothing suggests she knew England as a child.

B.why_wrong: The excerpt never says why she was sent to England or who decided it; it describes how she felt on arriving.

D.why_wrong: She does not hide her shyness: “forgetting both my manners and my good intentions,” she “burst into a flood of tears, and refused all comfort.”

sources.what: Angela Brazil, The Fortunes of Philippa, chapter II “My Cousins,” checked against Gutenberg 33387: the chapter's first sentence, then one sentence from the next paragraph (“I was so utterly weary ...”), with the intervening sentences omitted; Wikipedia (Angela Brazil): her first school story, The Fortunes of Philippa, was published in 1906

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1906). Key C. Literary purpose with one figurative image (the swallows), as in 2.9; A is the literalized image (LIT), D the reversed behavior (REV), B an invented reason (INV). Adapted: two sentences kept whole, the text between them omitted.

items.passage: To learn how a troop of olive baboons in central Kenya decides where to travel, Ariana Strandburg-Peshkin and colleagues fitted most of its members with high-resolution GPS collars and tracked each animal’s movements. <u>The baboons did not preferentially follow dominant individuals; instead, an animal was more likely to follow when several others set off in the same direction.</u> This pattern suggests that even in a society organized by a strict hierarchy, decisions about collective movement can be shared among many members of the group.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes a limitation of the tracking method mentioned in the previous sentence.
It presents findings that support the conclusion drawn in the following sentence.
It offers a hypothesis that the researchers tested using the approach described in the following sentence.
It explains why the researchers chose to study baboons rather than another species of primate.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence reports what the tracking revealed: the baboons “did not preferentially follow dominant individuals” but were “more likely to follow when several others set off in the same direction.” The following sentence draws a conclusion from that “pattern”: decisions “can be shared among many members of the group.” So the underlined sentence supplies findings that support the conclusion in the following sentence.

A.recipe: wrong relation to the previous sentence (REL)
A.why_wrong: The sentence reports what the collars revealed; it does not describe any shortcoming of the “high-resolution GPS collars.”

C.why_wrong: The sentence states results, not a hypothesis, and the following sentence gives an interpretation, not an approach; the approach is in the previous sentence.

D.why_wrong: The text never says why baboons were chosen or compares them with other primates.

sources.what: Strandburg-Peshkin, Farine, Couzin, Crofoot 2015, Science (PubMed abstract): high-resolution GPS tracking of wild baboons shows shared decision-making; rather than preferentially following dominant individuals, baboons are more likely to follow when multiple initiators agree; democratic collective action in a socially stratified society

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). Key B. Function family: local link (the span supports a claim in the next sentence), as in 2.1. REL siblings with previous and following pointers for A and C; D an invented motive. Kenya site (Mpala) left unnamed.

items.passage: Infants hear new words while surrounded by many objects, so it has been unclear how they determine which object a word refers to. <u>To view the world from an infant’s perspective, Elizabeth Clerkin, Linda Smith, and colleagues equipped babies between about eight and ten months old with small head-mounted cameras and recorded ordinary mealtimes in their homes.</u> Although the scenes were cluttered, a very small set of objects appeared again and again, a regularity that may make it considerably easier for infants to connect a word with the thing it names.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes the approach researchers used to address the problem presented in the previous sentence.
It presents a finding that challenges the explanation offered in the previous sentence.
It explains why infants learn the names of some objects sooner than the names of others.
It introduces a hypothesis about early word learning that the images described in the following sentence go on to contradict.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents a problem: “it has been unclear how they determine which object a word refers to.” The underlined sentence describes what the researchers did about it: they “equipped babies ... with small head-mounted cameras and recorded ordinary mealtimes in their homes.” The last sentence reports what the recordings showed. So the underlined sentence describes an approach used to address the problem in the previous sentence.

B.why_wrong: The underlined sentence reports a method, not a finding, and the previous sentence offers no explanation to challenge; it states that the matter “has been unclear.”

C.why_wrong: The sentence says nothing about which names infants learn sooner; it describes how the scenes were recorded.

D.why_wrong: The sentence states no hypothesis, and the images described next are not said to contradict anything; they reveal that “a very small set of objects appeared again and again.”

sources.what: Clerkin, Hart, Rehg, Yu, Smith 2017, Philosophical Transactions B (PubMed abstract): head camera video from 8½- to 10½-month-old infants at 147 at-home mealtimes; cluttered scenes, but a very small set of objects pervasively present, which may substantially reduce referential ambiguity in early word learning

items.notes: Area: social science (developmental psychology). Key A. Problem, method (the span), result, as in 2.20. Distractors: two REL labels (finding, hypothesis) and one INV. Elizabeth Clerkin is first author; Linda Smith is the senior author.

items.passage: Victor Hugo’s drawings are usually treated as a mere sideline to his novels and poems. That view sells them short. Hugo produced more than 4,000 drawings, predominantly in dark ink washes, and from 1848 to 1851, when he had set writing aside for politics, drawing was his exclusive creative outlet. His art should be counted among his principal achievements.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why Hugo temporarily stopped writing in the middle of his career
To describe the materials and methods Hugo used to make his drawings
To compare the reception of Hugo’s drawings during his lifetime with the reception of his novels and poems
To argue that Hugo’s drawings are more significant than they are commonly taken to be
items.explanation: The text opens with a common view, that Hugo’s drawings are “a mere sideline,” and rejects it: “That view sells them short.” It then gives evidence (“more than 4,000 drawings” and a period when “drawing was his exclusive creative outlet”) and concludes, “His art should be counted among his principal achievements.” The text argues that the drawings matter more than is usually assumed, as choice D says.

A.recipe: one detail taken as the purpose (PART)
A.why_wrong: The text mentions that Hugo “had set writing aside for politics,” but only as evidence of how important drawing was to him; explaining that decision is not its purpose.

B.recipe: one detail taken as the purpose (PART)
B.why_wrong: The text says only that the drawings were “predominantly in dark ink washes”; it does not describe his methods, and that detail serves the argument.

C.why_wrong: The text says the drawings are “usually treated as a mere sideline” but does not compare how audiences received the drawings and the writing.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Victor Hugo (Drawings): more than 4,000 drawings, about 3,000 surviving; usually dark brown or black pen-and-ink wash; drawing became more important shortly before his exile when he stopped writing to devote himself to politics, and was his exclusive creative outlet between 1848 and 1851

It introduces the woodcarver whose career is the main focus of the text.
It sets up the description of the cemetery that is presented in the sentences that follow.
It questions a belief about European cemeteries that the following sentences show to be widespread.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence names the cemetery in Săpânța and calls it “a striking exception” to the somber gravestones described first. The sentences that follow then describe it: its crosses are “brightly painted,” each with a “naive portrait” and an epitaph that is “frequently humorous.” So the underlined sentence sets up the description that follows.

A.why_wrong: The sentence does not add to the account of somber European gravestones; it introduces “a striking exception” to them.

B.recipe: content of a later sentence, wrong span (PART)

items.passage: By sequencing DNA from potato leaves preserved in herbarium collections since the 1840s, Kentaro Yoshida, Hernán Burbano, and colleagues reconstructed the genome of the strain of Phytophthora infestans responsible for the blight that triggered the Irish famine. items.passage: A common assumption has been that baleen whales attained enormous dimensions only after evolving baleen, which enables them to filter vast quantities of small prey from seawater. Ewan Fordyce and Felix Marx determined that the animal was roughly eight meters long but possessed sharp, abraded teeth and probably no baleen, suggesting that it captured prey by biting and suction.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents an assumption about how certain animals evolved, then describes a discovery that casts doubt on that assumption.
It describes a method for studying fossil skulls, then explains why that method has produced conflicting results.
It presents an assumption about how certain animals evolved, then describes a fossil that researchers now regard as the earliest whale known to have had baleen.
It identifies a gap in the fossil record of whales, then explains how a recent discovery has filled that gap.
items.explanation: The first sentence states an assumption: baleen whales “attained enormous dimensions only after evolving baleen.” The rest of the text describes a study of Llanocetus that “has complicated this picture”: the whale was “roughly eight meters long” but “probably” had “no baleen.” So the text presents an assumption and then a discovery that casts doubt on it.

B.why_wrong: The text mentions examining a skull but describes no method that has produced conflicting results.

C.recipe: first move right, second move reversed (REV)
C.why_wrong: The text says Llanocetus “probably” had “no baleen”; it does not present it as an early whale with baleen.

The following text is from Laura E. Richards’s 1897 novel Three Margarets. Three cousins who have never met before are riding together in a carriage.

The night was dark, and the carriage-lamps threw an uncertain gleam on the three figures leaning back in their corners, muffled and silent. The avenue was long,—interminably long, it seemed to one of the three travellers; and finally <u>the silence so oppressed her that she determined to conquer her shyness and break it</u>.

“What a very long avenue!” she said, speaking in a low, sweet voice.

There was no reply.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that one of the cousins is annoyed by the noise of the carriage.
It reveals the discomfort that leads one of the cousins to speak.
It indicates that one of the cousins is frightened by the darkness of the road.
It shows that the cousins quarreled with one another before the journey began.
items.explanation: The cousins sit “muffled and silent,” and “the silence so oppressed” one of them “that she determined to conquer her shyness and break it.” She then speaks: “What a very long avenue!” The underlined portion reveals the discomfort that makes her speak, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: What troubles her is “the silence,” not noise; the text never mentions the sound of the carriage.

C.recipe: a nearby detail misread as the feeling (LIT)
C.why_wrong: The night is “dark,” but the underlined portion says the silence oppressed her, not that she is afraid of the road.

D.why_wrong: The cousins “have never met before,” so they cannot have quarreled; their silence comes from shyness.

The following text is from Mabel Osgood Wright’s 1903 novel Aunt Jimmy’s Will. Bertha’s father has just been buried.

The little girl had been christened Bertha, after her grandmother, but as, from the time she could speak a word, she was always singing, her father had called her “Bird.” Yet this day the little bird in her throat was mute and only made a strange fluttering; so that the neighbours, talking in whispers as they drank the tea that a stout, rosy woman, who seemed to be in charge, was serving in the kitchen, said, “Poor child, if she’d only let go and cry it out natural, it would do her good; but that dry sobbing is enough to break a body’s heart.”
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how a girl came to be known by a nickname
To show that the neighbors disapprove of how a girl is behaving
To convey how deeply a girl is affected by her father’s death
To suggest that a girl is pretending to be sadder than she is
items.explanation: Bertha, called “Bird” because she “was always singing,” is now silent: “the little bird in her throat was mute and only made a strange fluttering.” The neighbors say her “dry sobbing is enough to break a body’s heart.” The text conveys the depth of her grief, as choice C says.

A.recipe: one sentence taken as the purpose (PART)
A.why_wrong: The first sentence explains the nickname “Bird,” but only to set up the image of her silence; the text as a whole is about her grief.

B.why_wrong: The neighbors pity her (“Poor child”); they wish she would cry because “it would do her good,” not because they disapprove.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests pretense. Her “dry sobbing” moves the neighbors, who think it “enough to break a body’s heart.”

items.passage: In 1980, Aaron Lansky was a twenty-four-year-old graduate student of Yiddish literature. He realized that irreplaceable Yiddish books were being discarded by American families who could no longer read the language of their parents and grandparents. To rescue them, he organized a nationwide network of volunteer collectors, known as zamlers. The organization he founded, now the Yiddish Book Center in Amherst, Massachusetts, has since recovered more than a million volumes. It has also used duplicate copies to establish or strengthen collections at more than 700 libraries, schools, and museums worldwide.

options: To provide an overview of how an effort to save books began and what it has accomplished
To explain why fewer people read Yiddish today than in earlier generations
To argue that more libraries should collect books written in Yiddish
To compare the Yiddish Book Center with other libraries in Massachusetts
items.explanation: The text describes how the effort began, when Lansky “realized that irreplaceable Yiddish books were being discarded” and “organized a nationwide network of volunteer collectors.” It then reports what the organization has achieved: it “has since recovered more than a million volumes” and has helped build collections at “more than 700 libraries, schools, and museums.” Choice A covers both parts.

B.recipe: one detail taken as the purpose (PART)
B.why_wrong: The text notes that some families “could no longer read the language,” but only to explain why books were being discarded; it does not explain a decline in readers.

C.recipe: neutral profile read as an argument (STANCE)
C.why_wrong: The text reports what the center has done; it never urges libraries to collect more Yiddish books.

items.passage: Saturn is wrapped in clouds that travel at different speeds, so astronomers cannot simply observe its surface to determine the length of its day. For decades, they relied instead on radio emissions from the planet. These signals repeated about every 10 hours and 39 minutes. <u>However, measurements by the Cassini spacecraft revealed that the timing of the signals had changed and did not correspond to the planet’s actual rotation.</u> In 2019, Christopher Mankovich and colleagues instead analyzed waves in Saturn’s rings that are generated by vibrations within the planet. From these waves, they calculated a day of about 10 hours and 34 minutes.

It summarizes earlier studies of the waves that vibrations inside Saturn produce in its rings.
It describes a problem with an earlier method of measuring the length of Saturn’s day.

The last two sentences describe a new approach.

B.recipe: content of the next sentence, misdescribed (PART)

D.why_wrong: Cassini’s measurements revealed the problem with the radio signals; the text does not criticize the spacecraft’s instruments.

items.passage: In many regions, boatbuilders once fastened their vessels together not with nails but by sewing. They drilled rows of holes along the edges of neighboring planks and stitched the planks together with cord. The cord was often coir, a rope made from coconut-husk fibers. The mtepe, a boat of East Africa’s Swahili coast, was assembled with coir and wooden pegs. It compares two methods of building boats, then argues that one method is superior to the other.

items.passage: Harbor seals are marine mammals, but a small population inhabits Alaska’s Iliamna Lake year-round. Because the lake is connected to the ocean by a 110-kilometer river, some researchers had hypothesized that seals regularly move between freshwater and marine habitats. Analyzing DNA extracted from seal scat and from tissue samples contributed by Indigenous hunters, Tatiana Ferrer and colleagues instead found the lake population to be genetically distinct from every marine population examined, including the nearest. Given the lake seals’ markedly reduced genetic diversity, a loss that would probably have required considerable time, the team concluded that the population has likely been isolated for an extended period.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It reports a surprising genetic pattern in a group of lake-dwelling animals and explains that the pattern shows the animals to be a different species from their relatives in the ocean.
It discusses a genetic study of a group of lake-dwelling animals in order to question whether samples contributed by hunters can reveal how those animals are related to others.
It presents an unexpected finding about a group of lake-dwelling animals and the reasoning behind researchers’ conclusion that the group has probably long been cut off from its relatives.
It presents an unexpected finding about a group of lake-dwelling animals and suggests that the group’s low genetic diversity indicates that it arrived in the lake from the ocean only recently.
items.explanation: Because the lake “is connected to the ocean by a 110-kilometer river,” some researchers expected seals to “regularly move between freshwater and marine habitats,” but Ferrer and colleagues “instead found the lake population to be genetically distinct from every marine population examined.” The text then gives the reasoning behind the team’s conclusion: the seals’ “markedly reduced genetic diversity” is “a loss that would probably have required considerable time,” so the population “has likely been isolated for an extended period.” Choice C names both the unexpected finding and that reasoning.

A.recipe: first clause true, later clause overreaches (BROAD)
A.why_wrong: The text does report a surprising genetic pattern, but it calls the lake seals “a small population” of harbor seals and never says they are a separate species. Its conclusion concerns how long the population “has likely been isolated,” not what species it belongs to.

B.why_wrong: The samples “contributed by Indigenous hunters” are simply part of the evidence the team analyzed. The text never questions what they can reveal; it reports what the DNA showed and what the team concluded from it.

D.recipe: first clause true, later clause reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The finding is unexpected, but the text draws the opposite conclusion from the low diversity: losing it “would probably have required considerable time,” so the population “has likely been isolated for an extended period” rather than having arrived recently.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Charles Lamb’s 1825 essay “The Superannuated Man.” The narrator has just retired after more than thirty years as a clerk.

For the first day or two I felt stunned, overwhelmed. I could only apprehend my felicity; I was too confused to taste it sincerely. I wandered about, thinking I was happy, and knowing that I was not. I could scarce trust myself with myself. From a poor man, poor in Time, I was suddenly lifted up into a vast revenue; I could see no end of my possessions; I wanted some steward, or judicious bailiff, to manage my estates in Time for me.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It conveys the narrator’s initial difficulty in enjoying a change of circumstances that he regards as fortunate.
It reveals the narrator’s growing suspicion that a change he had long hoped for has left him worse off than before.
It describes the narrator’s uncertainty about how to invest the money that he saved during his many years of work.
It presents the narrator’s attempt to convince himself that a change he had long dreaded has in fact turned out well.
items.explanation: The narrator calls his retirement “my felicity” and says he has been “lifted up into a vast revenue” of time, so he regards the change as fortunate. Yet “for the first day or two” he was “too confused to taste it sincerely,” wandering about “thinking I was happy, and knowing that I was not.” The text therefore conveys his early difficulty in enjoying a change he considers lucky, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The narrator is not yet happy, but he never suggests he is worse off. He calls the change “my felicity” and speaks of “a vast revenue,” and his confusion is limited to “the first day or two,” not a growing suspicion.

C.why_wrong: The “revenue,” “possessions,” and “estates” are figurative: he was “poor in Time” and is now rich in it, wanting a steward “to manage my estates in Time.” The text says nothing about money he saved.

D.why_wrong: The line “thinking I was happy, and knowing that I was not” describes confusion, not an effort at self-persuasion, and nothing in the text suggests he had dreaded retiring; he calls it “my felicity.”

items.passage: Soon after the metronome was patented in 1815, Beethoven added tempo markings to his eight published symphonies, and musicians have disputed them ever since: many consider the indicated tempos too fast to be performed well, while others insist that the markings express the composer’s wishes. Some have even blamed a faulty metronome. But analyzing 36 recorded performances by different conductors, Almudena Martín-Castro and Iñaki Ucar found that the performances ran slower than marked by a strikingly consistent margin—one that could result from reading the metronome’s scale below its sliding weight rather than above it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that conductors should finally adopt the tempos a composer marked, since research has shown that his metronome worked properly
To present research indicating that a long-standing disagreement over a composer’s instructions may stem from a simple misreading
To describe research showing that a faulty metronome led a composer to mark tempos considerably faster than he had intended
To explain why conductors in recent decades have chosen slower tempos for a composer’s symphonies than earlier conductors did
items.explanation: The text first describes a dispute: “many consider the indicated tempos too fast,” while “others insist that the markings express the composer’s wishes.” It then reports that Martín-Castro and Ucar found performances slower “by a strikingly consistent margin,” one that “could result from reading the metronome’s scale below its sliding weight rather than above it.” The text thus presents research suggesting that the dispute may come from a misreading, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The text does turn away from the “faulty metronome” explanation, but it never urges conductors to do anything. If anything, the finding suggests the markings are too fast because of a misreading, not that they should be followed.

C.why_wrong: The faulty metronome is the view the text sets aside (“Some have even blamed a faulty metronome. But...”). The researchers’ margin “could result from reading the metronome’s scale” wrongly, not from a defect in the device.

D.why_wrong: The study compares performances with Beethoven’s markings, not conductors of one period with those of another. The text never says tempos have changed over time.

sources.what: Martín-Castro and Ucar 2020, PLOS ONE (PubMed abstract; PMC7743971 full text): Beethoven added metronome marks to his eight published symphonies after Maelzel’s 1815 patent; many musicians consider them too quick, others claim them as his will; tempos extracted from 36 recordings by different conductors show a systematic deviation (always slower on average, about 12 bpm); the model of Maelzel’s metronome rules out the broken-metronome hypothesis; the hasty marks could be explained by reading the scale below the weight instead of above
