items.passage: Owls combine sharp vision in dim light with acute hearing to hunt in darkness, but such sensory adaptations were long unknown among nonavian dinosaurs. <u>Examining features of the eyes and inner ears of living and extinct species, Jonah Choiniere and colleagues found that Shuvuuia deserti, a small Late Cretaceous dinosaur from Mongolia, had vision suited to extremely low light and hearing that rivaled the barn owl’s.</u> The researchers concluded that Shuvuuia probably hunted at night, and that this combination of abilities arose in dinosaurs long before modern birds appeared.

It describes a method of studying fossils that the following sentence suggests produced unreliable results.
It presents findings that support the conclusion about Shuvuuia’s behavior stated in the following sentence.

The following text is adapted from Samuel Butler’s 1903 novel The Way of All Flesh. Theobald Pontifex is the clergyman of Battersby, a country parish.

Who so integer vitæ scelerisque purus [blameless], it was asked, as Mr Pontifex of Battersby? Who so fit to be consulted if any difficulty about parish management should arise? Who such a happy mixture of the sincere uninquiring Christian and of the man of the world? For so people actually called him. They said he was such an admirable man of business. His constitutional timidity rendered him incapable of an attempt to overreach [cheat] when there was the remotest chance of opposition or publicity, and his correct bearing and somewhat stern expression were a great protection to him against being overreached.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It reports the high opinion that the people around Theobald hold of him and then identifies traits of his that help account for that opinion.
It reports the high opinion that the people around Theobald hold of him and then recounts the business dealings that first earned him that opinion.
It describes the suspicion with which Theobald is regarded in Battersby and then explains the steps he takes to overcome it.
It contrasts Theobald’s reputation in his parish with his reputation in his own family and then suggests which of the two is more accurate.
items.explanation: The first five sentences give what people say of Theobald: no one is so blameless or so “fit to be consulted,” he is “such a happy mixture” of Christian and man of the world, “such an admirable man of business.” The last sentence names traits behind that view: his “constitutional timidity” keeps him from cheating, and “his correct bearing and somewhat stern expression” keep others from cheating him. Choice A describes this structure.

B.why_wrong: People call him “an admirable man of business,” but the text recounts no business dealings; it names his timidity, bearing, and expression.

C.why_wrong: Theobald is admired, not suspected: “Who so integer vitæ scelerisque purus [blameless], it was asked, as Mr Pontifex of Battersby?”

D.why_wrong: The text gives only the opinion of the people around him; his family is never mentioned.

sources.what: Samuel Butler, The Way of All Flesh (1903), chapter XXIII, Project Gutenberg 2084: the paragraph beginning “Who so integer vitæ scelerisque purus,” sentences 1 to 5 and 7 copied exactly (the sentence on paying debts on time left out; two bracketed glosses added; italics of the Latin not shown)

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1903). Key A. Two-move structure as in 2.22 (the regard, then what sustains it); Butler’s irony is left to the student, and no option claims the opinion is mistaken. B keeps move one and invents move two, as more than a third of medium S distractors do.

fixes: excerpt checked against Gutenberg 2084 (sentences 1 to 5 and 7 exact, the debt sentence left out as noted)

items.passage:
The following text is from Dhan Gopal Mukerji’s 1922 book Kari the Elephant. The narrator, a boy in India, has been given a five-month-old elephant named Kari to take care of.

Every day I used to take him to the river in the morning for his bath. He would lie down on the sand bank while I rubbed him with the clean sand of the river for an hour. After that he would lie in the water for a long time. <u>On coming out his skin would be shining like ebony, and he would squeal with pleasure as I rubbed water down his back.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that Kari dislikes being led out of the river.
It shows how much Kari enjoys the care the narrator gives him.
It explains why the narrator uses sand rather than water to clean Kari.
It reveals the narrator’s relief that a tiring daily chore is finished.
items.explanation: In the underlined sentence, Kari’s skin is “shining like ebony” after his bath, and he “would squeal with pleasure” as the narrator rubs water down his back. These details show how much Kari enjoys the narrator’s care, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: Kari comes out of the water and squeals “with pleasure”; nothing suggests he dislikes leaving the river.

C.why_wrong: The narrator uses both sand and water, and the text never explains why he uses one rather than the other.

D.recipe: feeling given to the wrong character (SWAP)
D.why_wrong: The pleasure in the sentence is Kari’s, and the narrator never calls the bath tiring or expresses relief.

sources.what: Dhan Gopal Mukerji, Kari the Elephant (E. P. Dutton, 1922), chapter I, “Bringing Up Kari,” Project Gutenberg 24460: four consecutive sentences copied exactly; the chapter opens “Kari, the elephant, was five months old when he was given to me to take care of”

items.notes: Literature (children’s book, 1922). Key B. Literary-effect function as in 1.1 and 1.20; distractors REV, INV, SWAP. The underlined sentence ends the excerpt, and its simile (“shining like ebony”) is not literalized by any option.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Edward Bok’s 1920 autobiography The Americanization of Edward Bok, which Bok wrote in the third person. Edward, a boy whose family has recently immigrated from the Netherlands, is standing outside a bakery near his home.

The owner of the bakery, who had just placed in the window a series of trays filled with buns, tarts, and pies, came outside to look at the display. He found the hungry boy wistfully regarding the tempting-looking wares. “Look pretty good, don’t they?” asked the baker. “They would,” answered the Dutch boy with his national passion for cleanliness, “if your window were clean.” “That’s so, too,” mused the baker. “Perhaps you’ll clean it.” “I will,” was the laconic [brief] reply. And Edward Bok, there and then, got his first job.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why the bakery had recently lost many of its customers
To describe a boy’s disappointment at being turned away by a shop owner
To recount how a boy’s frank remark to a shop owner led to his first job
To compare the foods sold in American bakeries with those in the boy’s homeland
items.explanation: Edward tells the baker that his pastries would look good “if your window were clean.” The baker answers, “Perhaps you’ll clean it,” Edward agrees, and “there and then” he “got his first job.” The text recounts how a frank remark led to Edward’s first job, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The text never mentions the bakery’s customers or any loss of business.

B.why_wrong: Edward is not turned away; the baker invites him to clean the window, and Edward “got his first job.”

D.why_wrong: The text describes only the baker’s “buns, tarts, and pies”; it never mentions foods from the Netherlands.

sources.what: Edward Bok, The Americanization of Edward Bok (1920), chapter II, “The First Job: Fifty Cents a Week,” Project Gutenberg 3538: from “The owner of the bakery” to “got his first job,” copied exactly (straight quotation marks set as curly, one bracketed gloss added); Bok came to Brooklyn from the Netherlands as a boy

items.notes: Literature (autobiography, 1920). Key C. Easy purpose as in 1.17 and 1.5: the key names what happens; distractors INV, REV, INV (compare). The autobiography is in the third person, which the context line says.

fixes: excerpt checked against Gutenberg 3538 (contiguous, exact); context confirmed

items.passage: The Anacostia Community Museum opened in 1967 in the Anacostia neighborhood of Washington, D.C. The Smithsonian Institution established it to bring some of the resources of its museums on the National Mall into the neighborhood, hoping that the new museum would also encourage local residents to visit the main museums. It became the first federally funded community museum in the United States. Today, its exhibitions focus on the history and culture of the communities surrounding Anacostia, and it also houses a library.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To compare the Anacostia Community Museum with the Smithsonian’s museums on the National Mall
To argue that more neighborhoods should have museums devoted to local history
To explain why the Anacostia Community Museum moved into a larger building
To give an overview of the founding and focus of the Anacostia Community Museum
items.explanation: The text tells when and why the museum was founded: it “opened in 1967,” and the Smithsonian “established it to bring some of the resources of its museums on the National Mall into the neighborhood.” It then notes that it was “the first federally funded community museum in the United States” and that “its exhibitions focus on the history and culture of the communities surrounding Anacostia.” Choice D sums up this overview.

A.why_wrong: The museums on the National Mall are mentioned only to explain why the museum was created; the text never compares them with it.

B.why_wrong: The text describes one museum; it never argues that other neighborhoods should have museums.

C.why_wrong: The text never mentions the museum moving or its building.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Anacostia Community Museum: a Smithsonian community museum in the Anacostia neighborhood of Washington, D.C.; the first federally funded community museum in the United States; founded in 1967 to bring aspects of the Smithsonian museums on the National Mall to Anacostia, with the hope that residents would visit the main museums; focuses on the community in and around Anacostia; houses a library

items.notes: Area: humanities (museums, history). Key D. Easy profile as in 1.6 (“an overview of the history and importance”); key reworded. Distractors INV (compare), STANCE (argue), INV.

fixes: core claim confirmed (Wikipedia, Anacostia Community Museum)
plained toward CB: “extend” to “bring”, “the new institution” to “the new museum”, “concentrate on” to “focus on”; explanation quotes updated

items.passage: Iranian-born architect Nader Khalili devoted much of his career to designing inexpensive shelters from local materials, particularly for people displaced by war or natural disasters. His best-known method, which he called Superadobe, uses long fabric tubes filled with earth. Builders stack the tubes in successive layers, separated by strands of barbed wire that keep them from shifting, and the walls gradually curve inward to form a dome. Khalili’s designs drew on the traditional earthen houses of Iran’s deserts.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a debate between two architects and then explains how it was settled.
It introduces an architect and then describes the building method he is best known for.
It explains a traditional building technique and then lists several architects who use it.
It presents an architect’s early designs and then explains why he gave them up.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Nader Khalili, an architect who designed “inexpensive shelters.” The rest of the text describes “his best-known method,” Superadobe: earth-filled fabric tubes stacked “in successive layers, separated by strands of barbed wire.” Choice B describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: Only one architect is named, and the text describes no debate.

C.why_wrong: Superadobe is Khalili’s own method, and no other architects are named.

D.recipe: first move partly right, second invented (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text describes Khalili’s “best-known method,” not early designs he abandoned.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Superadobe: an earthbag technique developed by Iranian architect Nader Khalili, using layered long fabric tubes or bags filled with earth to form beehive-shaped corbelled domes; barbed wire between layers; refugee shelters built with UNDP and UNHCR; and Wikipedia, Nader Khalili: shelters from atypical materials for the developing world and emergencies; influenced by traditional arid house designs of Iran
Wikipedia, Nader Khalili

items.notes: Area: humanities (architecture). Key B. Easy structure as in 1.13 and 1.19 (person, then work); every distractor a different whole template, as easy S items use.

fixes: core claim confirmed (Wikipedia, Superadobe and Nader Khalili)

items.passage: Birds and mammals keep their bodies warm by producing heat internally. <u>This capacity is known as “endothermy.”</u> Most reptiles lack it and depend instead on outside sources of heat, such as sunlight. But biologist Glenn Tattersall and his colleagues discovered a surprising exception. During their breeding season, tegu lizards in South America kept their bodies as much as 10°C warmer than their surroundings at night. Like birds and mammals, the lizards did this by producing more heat and conserving it.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes a method that Tattersall’s team used to measure the lizards’ temperatures.
It explains why most reptiles depend on sunlight to stay warm.
It names a capacity that the text goes on to discuss in relation to tegu lizards.
It presents a claim that Tattersall’s team later showed to be false.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence gives a name, “endothermy,” to the capacity described in the first sentence: “producing heat internally.” The rest of the text discusses that capacity, noting that “most reptiles lack it” and that tegu lizards, surprisingly, showed it during their breeding season. Choice C describes this function.

A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence names a capacity; the text never describes how the team measured temperatures.

B.why_wrong: The following sentence says reptiles “depend instead on outside sources of heat,” but the underlined sentence only names the ability, and neither sentence explains why.

D.why_wrong: The underlined sentence is a definition, not a claim, and Tattersall’s team found tegus doing what it describes rather than showing anything false.

sources.what: Tattersall et al. 2016, Science Advances (PubMed abstract): small ectotherms usually cannot sustain body temperature well above ambient; tegu lizards sustained nighttime body temperatures up to 10°C above ambient during the reproductive season, through increased metabolic rate and decreased thermal conductance, the mechanisms of the “true endotherms,” birds and mammals

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal physiology). Key C. Easy F_term as in 1.11 (a term the rest of the text uses); the span and the key are worded away from the model (“This ability is known as”; “names an ability”). Tegus of the study are Salvator merianae, a South American species.

fixes: core claim confirmed (PubMed 26844295)

items.passage: Do koalas need to drink water? <u>A study led by Valentina Mella suggests that they do, particularly in hot, dry weather.</u> Because koalas obtain most of their moisture from the eucalyptus leaves they consume, researchers long assumed that drinking was largely unnecessary for them. But when Mella’s team installed water stations for wild koalas in New South Wales, Australia, the animals used them regularly throughout the year. Visits were more frequent on hot days, and the longer the interval since rainfall, the more time the koalas spent drinking.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It gives an answer to the question asked in the previous sentence.
It defines a term that is explained further in the following sentence.
It describes a problem that Mella’s study was unable to solve.
It explains why koalas prefer eucalyptus leaves to other foods.
items.explanation: The first sentence asks, “Do koalas need to drink water?” The underlined sentence answers it: a study led by Mella “suggests that they do, particularly in hot, dry weather.” The rest of the text gives the evidence. Choice A describes this function.

B.why_wrong: The underlined sentence defines no term; it reports what a study suggests.

C.why_wrong: The text presents the study’s findings and mentions nothing it failed to solve.

D.why_wrong: Eucalyptus leaves are mentioned later as a source of moisture; the text never says why koalas eat them or compares them with other foods.

sources.what: Mella et al. 2019, PLOS ONE (PubMed abstract): arboreal folivores rely on leaf moisture; artificial water stations (ground and tree drinkers) for koalas in New South Wales; first evidence of regular use of free water; used throughout the year; more time drinking the more days since rain; more frequent visits when temperature was high
Mella et al. 2020, Ethology (Crossref abstract): koalas are thought to have little need to drink because they gain most of their water from leaves

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). Key A. Easy F_answer as in 1.18: a question, then the underlined answer, then the evidence; distractors REL, REL, INV with valid pointers.

fixes: core claim confirmed (PubMed 31141564)

items.passage: In 2005, Japan’s Ministry of the Environment launched a campaign called Cool Biz to reduce the electricity that offices consume for air-conditioning. Government offices set their air conditioners at 28°C (82°F) during the summer months, and employees were encouraged to leave their jackets and ties at home so that they could work comfortably at that temperature. The campaign soon spread to private companies. The ministry estimated that Cool Biz reduced carbon dioxide emissions by 460,000 tons in 2005 and by 1.14 million tons in 2006.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To compare Japan’s approach to saving energy with the approaches taken by other countries
To argue that companies should require employees to dress formally even in hot weather
To describe how a relaxed office dress code made Japanese employees more productive
To describe a Japanese campaign to cut office energy use and its reported results
items.explanation: The text describes the campaign’s aim, “to reduce the electricity that offices consume for air-conditioning,” and its measures: air conditioners set “at 28°C” and employees encouraged “to leave their jackets and ties at home.” It ends with the ministry’s estimate that Cool Biz “reduced carbon dioxide emissions by 460,000 tons in 2005 and by 1.14 million tons in 2006.” Choice D sums up the effort and its reported results.

A.why_wrong: No other country is mentioned; the campaign spread only from government offices to “private companies” in Japan.

B.why_wrong: The text describes employees being encouraged “to leave their jackets and ties at home”; it argues for nothing, least of all formal dress.

C.why_wrong: The dress code is part of the campaign, but the result the text reports is lower carbon dioxide emissions, not productivity.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Cool Biz campaign: launched by Japan’s Ministry of the Environment in mid-2005 to reduce electricity consumption by limiting air conditioning; standard office air-conditioner temperature set to 28°C with a liberal summer dress code (no jackets or ties) so staff could work at that temperature; spread to the private sector; the ministry estimated a 460,000-ton CO2 reduction in 2005 and 1.14 million tons in 2006

items.notes: Area: social science (energy policy). Key D. Easy effort-and-results as in 1.8 (Portland); key worded away from the model’s “an effort ... and some results of that effort.” Replaces a Paris schoolyards draft that twinned a live RS item on hot asphalt schoolyards.

fixes: core claim confirmed (Wikipedia, Cool Biz campaign: 28°C, 2005, private sector, 460,000 and 1.14 million tons)

items.passage: Fire, fragmentation, and severe drought have thinned the canopy across extensive stretches of the southern Amazon, and whether such degraded forests regenerate depends partly on whether seeds can reach them. Working in Mato Grosso, Brazil, ecologist Lucas Paolucci and colleagues combined camera traps, dung surveys, and airborne lidar to monitor the lowland tapir (Tapirus terrestris), a large fruit-eating mammal. Tapirs, the researchers found, traveled and defecated more frequently in degraded forest than in undisturbed forest, depositing roughly three times as many seeds per hectare there.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes a study that tracked a large mammal through damaged and undisturbed forests and explains why the animal avoids places where the canopy is still closed.
It presents research showing that seeds carried by a large mammal sprout and grow more quickly in damaged forests than they do in undisturbed ones.
It discusses a study whose results suggest that a large mammal may help damaged forests recover by moving seeds into the places that most need them.
It explains how researchers used several methods to count a large mammal’s population and reports that the species itself is recovering in damaged forests.
items.explanation: The text opens by noting that the recovery of degraded Amazon forests “depends partly on whether seeds can reach them.” It then reports that tapirs “traveled and defecated more frequently in degraded forest than in undisturbed forest, depositing roughly three times as many seeds per hectare there.” Together these sentences present a study suggesting that tapirs may aid the recovery of damaged forests by carrying seeds into them, as choice C says.

A.recipe: first clause true, later clause invents a reason (INV)
A.why_wrong: The researchers did follow tapirs through both kinds of forest, but the text never says why the animals spend more time in degraded forest, and it never says they avoid closed canopy; it reports only where they “traveled and defecated more frequently.”

B.recipe: right elements, finding changed from seed numbers to seedling growth (INV)
B.why_wrong: The study counted how many seeds tapirs deposited (“roughly three times as many seeds per hectare”); the text says nothing about how quickly those seeds sprout or grow.

D.recipe: method partly right, recovery shifted from the forest to the animal (SWAP)
D.why_wrong: The methods tracked where tapirs went, not how many there are, and the recovery the text discusses is that of the forests (“whether such degraded forests regenerate”), not of the tapir population.

sources.what: Paolucci, Pereira, Rattis, Silvério, Marques, Macedo, Brando 2019, Biotropica 51: 245–252, “Lowland tapirs facilitate seed dispersal in degraded Amazonian forests” (Dryad record with abstract): tapirs travel and defecate more often in degraded forests, about 9,822 vs 2,950 seeds per ha per year; may contribute to natural forest regeneration; camera traps, field surveys and lidar in Mato Grosso

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology). Key C. Band 6 (P_study, as d4732483): key paraphrases the passage’s link between seed supply and recovery (“moving seeds into the places that most need them”) instead of echoing “disperse”; the passage leaves the recovery claim implicit, so the key needs both the first and last sentences. A and D open with a true account of the method and fail on a later clause; B keeps the elements and changes the measured outcome. Ratio rounded from 9,822 vs 2,950 seeds per hectare per year (3.3x).

band7.why: P_study on d4732483 (band 6): the key needs the first sentence’s seed-supply premise and the last sentence’s finding, paraphrased (“places that most need them”); A and D open true and fail later, B changes the measured outcome. One finding with a hedge, not the dual purpose band 7 needs.

items.passage:
The following text is from Leslie Pinckney Hill’s 1921 poem “Summer Magic.”

So many cares to vex the day,
So many fears to haunt the night,
My heart was all but weaned away
From every lure of old delight.
Then summer came, announced by June,
With beauty, miracle and mirth.
She hung aloft the rounding moon,
She poured her sunshine on the earth,
She drove the sap and broke the bud,
She set the crimson rose afire.
She stirred again my sullen blood,
And waked in me a new desire.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To illustrate the speaker’s growing fear that the beauty summer has brought will vanish as suddenly as it first appeared
To convey how the arrival of a season restored the speaker’s ability to take pleasure in life after a troubled time
To show how the speaker overcame a troubled period by deliberately seeking out the beauty of the natural world
To suggest that the speaker’s worries were caused by the hardships of the season that came before summer
items.explanation: The first four lines describe a time when “cares” and “fears” had left the speaker’s heart “all but weaned away / From every lure of old delight.” Then “summer came,” and the season “stirred again my sullen blood, / And waked in me a new desire.” The poem thus conveys how summer’s arrival revived the speaker’s capacity for joy after a period of trouble, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The “fears” belong to the troubled time before summer; once summer arrives the speaker describes only its gifts and his own revival, never a fear that its beauty will vanish.

C.recipe: first part true, agent swapped from the season to the speaker (SWAP)
C.why_wrong: The speaker does move past a troubled time, but not by seeking anything out: the heart had been “all but weaned away / From every lure of old delight” until summer acted on it (“She stirred again my sullen blood, / And waked in me a new desire”).

D.why_wrong: The poem says the cares came “to vex the day” and the fears “to haunt the night,” but it never names their source or ties them to an earlier season.

sources.what: Leslie Pinckney Hill, The Wings of Oppression (Boston: Stratford, 1921), “Summer Magic” (lines 1–12); text checked against The Book of American Negro Poetry (1922), Gutenberg 11986; the 1921 collection confirmed as the poem’s source in the Lehigh full-text edition
full text of The Wings of Oppression (1921), contents list includes “Summer Magic”

items.notes: Literature (poem, 1921). Key B. Band 6 as 3.19 and 3.15 (poems whose key names a two-part feeling): the key joins the troubled time and the revival, so an option that names only one half fails. Excerpt is the poem’s first 12 lines (of 28), cut at the end of a sentence; indentation of alternate lines dropped as in CB poem items. A takes the word “fears” for the wrong time, C invents celebrants, D invents a cause.

fixes: C (invented celebrants, wholly off) replaced by an agency swap that keeps the true first part (the speaker overcomes a troubled time) and fails on who acts

band7.why: P_lit on 3.19 and 3.15 (band 6): two-part feeling (troubled time, then revival by the season); after the fix A, C and D each keep part of the poem (fears, the troubled time, an earlier season) and fail on one link. Plain 1921 diction keeps it below the archaic band-7 P_lit model b0f7541b.

items.passage: Historians long treated the food riots of eighteenth-century England as little more than reflexes of hunger, outbursts by crowds driven to desperation when bread grew scarce, but in a 1971 essay the social historian E. P. Thompson rejected that interpretation. <u>Rioters, he observed, were often notably restrained: instead of simply plundering, crowds typically demanded that grain be sold at the price that local custom considered fair.</u> Such discipline, Thompson argued, reflected a “moral economy,” a widely held conviction that dealers owed obligations to their communities and that profiting from scarcity was illegitimate.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reports a tendency among the crowds that earlier historians had cited as proof that hunger alone drove the riots.
It identifies the economic pressures that, according to Thompson, made grain dealers unwilling to lower their prices during periods of scarcity and unrest.
It offers an example of the disorder that Thompson concedes sometimes weakened the crowds’ claims to be acting on behalf of their communities.
It describes a pattern in the rioters’ conduct that Thompson uses as evidence for his challenge to an earlier explanation of the riots.
items.explanation: The text says historians treated the riots as “reflexes of hunger” and that Thompson “rejected that interpretation.” The underlined sentence reports what he observed instead: rioters “were often notably restrained” and “demanded that grain be sold at the price that local custom considered fair.” The last sentence then says this “discipline” reflected a “moral economy,” so the underlined sentence supplies the evidence for Thompson’s challenge, as choice D says.

A.recipe: first clause true, evidence given to the wrong side (SWAP)
A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence does report the crowds’ conduct, but it is Thompson’s observation, offered against the hunger view; the text never says earlier historians cited this restraint, and restraint would not support a view of the riots as desperate “outbursts.”

B.why_wrong: The sentence is about what the crowds did and demanded, not about pressures on dealers; the text mentions dealers only in the last sentence, as people who “owed obligations to their communities.”

C.why_wrong: The sentence stresses the crowds’ restraint (“notably restrained,” “instead of simply plundering”), not disorder, and Thompson concedes nothing in the text; he uses the restraint to support his argument.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Moral economy: concept developed by E. P. Thompson in his 1971 essay “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century”; riots not just a response to physical hunger; generally peaceable events demanding that prices be set according to traditional norms, a traditional “fair price”; profiteering on necessities seen as immoral

items.notes: Area: history (social history). Key D. Band 6 (F_example, as ac9a3a26): the span is an example whose job depends on the sentences around it (the view it answers and the claim it supports). A matches the key’s first clause in substance (the crowds’ conduct) and fails on who used the evidence; C flips the stance; B moves to the wrong party. The span paraphrases the source’s “generally peaceable events demanding that the prices ... be set according to” custom; no detail beyond the source is added.

band7.why: F_example on ac9a3a26 (band 6): the span is a means (evidence for a challenge to the hunger view) and A shares the key’s first clause, failing on who used the evidence; written to band_target 6 and a fair strong 6.

items.passage: Flash photography is prohibited around seahorses in many aquariums and restricted at some dive sites, on the assumption that intense flashes harm the animals. To test that assumption, marine ecologist Maarten De Brauwer and colleagues exposed captive seahorses to underwater strobes fired at maximum strength, considerably brighter than an ordinary camera flash, and found no detectable damage to the animals’ eyes and no reduction in their success at capturing prey. In the team’s other trials, however, divers who handled fish to obtain a better photograph provoked pronounced stress responses.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It presents research suggesting that a widely adopted precaution meant to protect certain animals may target a smaller risk to them than another kind of human behavior poses.
It presents research on how certain animals respond to divers in order to argue that flash photography should be allowed wherever those animals are found.
It describes an experiment that tested a common assumption about certain animals and explains why their eyes are less sensitive to bright light than researchers had expected.
It describes research on the effects of photography on certain animals and suggests that the rules limiting flashes at aquariums and dive sites have reduced the harm that divers cause them.
items.explanation: The text begins with a widespread rule, the ban on flash photography around seahorses, which rests on “the assumption that intense flashes harm the animals.” De Brauwer’s team found “no detectable damage to the animals’ eyes and no reduction in their success at capturing prey,” even with strobes “fired at maximum strength,” while divers who handled fish “provoked pronounced stress responses.” The text therefore presents research suggesting that the precaution targets a smaller risk than handling does, as choice A says.

B.recipe: first clause true, stance flipped to an argument with an overreach (STANCE)
B.why_wrong: The text reports findings without arguing for any policy, and it gives no grounds for allowing flashes in every place where seahorses live; the team’s only finding about divers is that handling fish caused stress.

C.recipe: first clause true, later clause invents an explanation (INV)
C.why_wrong: The experiment did test a common assumption, but the text reports only that the flashes caused no detectable eye damage; it never explains how sensitive the eyes are or says what researchers had expected about that.

D.recipe: first clause true, later clause invents an effect of the rules (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text describes the research accurately at first, but it never measures what flash rules have achieved; it says only that the rules rest on an assumption the study did not support.

sources.what: De Brauwer, Gordon, Shalders, Saunders, Archer, Harvey, Collin, Partridge, McIlwain 2019, Scientific Reports 9: 748 (PubMed abstract): photographic flashes did not change gross ocular and retinal anatomy of seahorses and did not alter feeding success; physical manipulation of animals by photographing scuba divers elicited strong stress responses

items.passage: In the 1970s, seismologist Hiroo Kanamori identified a serious deficiency in the magnitude scales then in use, which estimated an earthquake’s size from the amplitude of the seismic waves recorded by instruments. Because those waves stop growing once a rupture becomes very large, the scales saturated: the 1960 earthquake in Chile, vastly more powerful than other earthquakes rated near 8, registered only about 8.5. With seismologist Thomas Hanks, Kanamori subsequently defined the moment magnitude scale, which is calculated instead from the area of the fault that slips and the distance it moves.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a problem that a researcher identified with existing measurement scales and then explains how he adjusted those scales so that they could register larger seismic waves.
It outlines an objection that a researcher raised to certain measuring tools and then explains why other scientists kept relying on those tools anyway.
It presents a researcher’s criticism of an established way of measuring something and then describes an alternative that he helped develop to overcome that weakness.
It describes a researcher’s attempt to measure a well-known event and then explains how the results confirmed the accuracy of the scale used at the time.
items.explanation: The first two sentences present Kanamori’s criticism: scales based on “the amplitude of the seismic waves” “saturated,” so the “vastly more powerful” 1960 Chile earthquake “registered only about 8.5.” The last sentence describes his response, the moment magnitude scale, “calculated instead from the area of the fault that slips and the distance it moves.” The text thus presents a criticism and then an alternative developed to address it, as choice C says.

A.recipe: first move right, second move turned into a repair of the old method (INV)
A.why_wrong: Kanamori did identify a problem with the older scales, but he did not adjust them to register bigger waves: the text says those waves “stop growing” once a rupture becomes very large, and the new scale is “calculated instead from the area of the fault that slips and the distance it moves.”

B.recipe: first move right, later move invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: The text does present Kanamori’s objection to the older scales, but it never says other scientists kept using them; it ends with the new scale that he and Hanks defined.

D.recipe: example misread as the purpose, outcome reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The Chile earthquake is an example of the flaw, not an event Kanamori set out to measure, and its low rating shows that the older scale was inaccurate for very large earthquakes, not that it was confirmed.

Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori; Kanamori recognized the deficiency that amplitude-based scales saturate (Ms saturates around 8.0, underestimating the 1960 Chilean earthquake, Ms about 8.5 vs Mw about 9.5); seismic moment is a measure of the fault slip and area

The following text is from Edward Noyes Westcott’s 1898 novel David Harum. John Lenox, a young man who spent much of his childhood away from home, has recently returned to live with his father in New York City.

But as time went on even John’s unwatchful eye could not fail to notice that all was not well with his father. Haggard lines were multiplying in the quiet face, and the silence at the dinner table was often unbroken except by John’s unfruitful efforts to keep some sort of a conversation in motion. More and more frequently it occurred that his father would retire to his own room immediately after dinner was over, and the food on his plate would be almost untouched, while he took more wine than had ever been his habit.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why a character’s father has begun to avoid conversations about his business
To describe a character’s frustration at his father’s refusal to eat meals with him
To suggest that a character has long known that his father is in financial trouble
To portray a character’s dawning awareness of worrying changes in his father’s behavior
items.explanation: The text says that “even John’s unwatchful eye could not fail to notice that all was not well with his father,” then lists what he sees: “Haggard lines” in his father’s face, silent dinners, early retreats to his room, food “almost untouched,” and “more wine than had ever been his habit.” The text thus portrays John’s growing awareness of troubling changes in his father, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The father is silent at dinner, but the text gives no reason for his behavior and never mentions his business.

B.why_wrong: The father does sit at dinner with John; he leaves “immediately after dinner was over.” The text also never says John is frustrated; it describes his “unfruitful efforts” to keep a conversation going.

C.why_wrong: The text stresses that John notices only “as time went on” and despite his “unwatchful eye”; it says nothing about money or about long-standing knowledge.

sources.what: Edward Noyes Westcott, David Harum: A Story of American Life (1898), chapter X, checked against Gutenberg 17617; three consecutive sentences copied exactly; John Lenox lives with his father in New York

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1898). Key D. Character’s perception of another’s distress, as 2.7 portrays a reaction to a new setting. A invents a cause, B and C reverse details the text states (“after dinner was over,” “as time went on”).

items.passage:
The following text is from Sabine Baring-Gould’s 1880 novel Mehalah: A Story of the Salt Marshes. Mehalah, who is also called Glory, lives with her mother, Mrs. Sharland, on an isolated farm in the salt marshes of Essex, England. George De Witt, the young man she loves, has disappeared and may be dead.

It is the way with strong natures to allow their griefs no expression, to hide their sorrows and mask their wounds. Glory did not speak of George. She did not weep. She made no lamentation over his loss; more wonderful still in her mother’s eyes, she uttered no reproaches against anyone for it. A weak nature always exhausts its troubles in reproaches of others; a strong one eats out its own heart. Mehalah listened with a dull ear to her mother’s murmurs, and made no response. Mrs. Sharland set her down as unfeeling.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To show that a character’s silence about her loss reflects the depth of her feeling, which her mother fails to recognize
To contrast a character’s silent grief with her mother’s open weeping over the disappearance of the young man
To suggest that a character’s mother admires the calm way her daughter has accepted a loss
To explain why a character has stopped grieving for a young man she once loved
items.explanation: The text says that “strong natures” hide “their sorrows and mask their wounds,” and that Glory accordingly “did not speak of George” or weep; “a strong one eats out its own heart.” Her mother, however, “set her down as unfeeling.” The text thus shows that Mehalah’s silence reflects deep feeling that her mother misreads, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: Mehalah’s silence is set beside her mother’s “murmurs,” but the text never says the mother weeps or what her murmurs are about.

C.why_wrong: Mrs. Sharland does not admire her daughter’s calm; she “set her down as unfeeling.”

D.why_wrong: Mehalah has not stopped grieving: like other “strong natures,” she hides her sorrow, and “a strong one eats out its own heart.”

sources.what: Sabine Baring-Gould, Mehalah: A Story of the Salt Marshes (1880; Smith, Elder new edition 1884), Gutenberg 54404: seven consecutive sentences copied exactly; Mehalah (called Glory) lives with her mother at the Ray in the Essex marshes; George De Witt, whom she loves, has disappeared

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1880). Key A. Two-part key (silence as a sign of deep feeling, and the mother’s misreading), the medium step up from a one-part feeling as in 2.9. B keeps the contrast with the mother and invents its other half; C reverses the mother’s judgment and D the daughter’s feeling. Context line names Glory as Mehalah and Mrs. Sharland as her mother so the excerpt’s three names are clear.

items.passage: Commodity prices are among the most difficult kinds of economic information to recover for the ancient world, because few records of everyday commerce survive; Babylonia is a notable exception. For roughly six centuries, beginning around 650 BCE, scribes there compiled what are now called the Astronomical Diaries, clay tablets documenting nightly observations of the Moon and planets. <u>Every month, the scribes also recorded the level of the Euphrates River and the market value of barley, dates, wool, and several other commodities.</u> These entries, preserved on several hundred surviving tablets, provide historians with an unusually extensive and detailed record of prices in an ancient city.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains how the scribes carried out the nightly observations of the Moon and planets that are mentioned in the previous sentence.
It describes a feature of certain records that explains why Babylonia is an exception to a pattern noted earlier in the text.
It suggests that the scribes considered the city’s markets more important than the movements of objects in the sky.
It introduces a weakness of the tablets that the following sentence goes on to describe in more detail.
items.explanation: The text begins by saying that “few records of everyday commerce survive” from the ancient world and that “Babylonia is a notable exception.” The underlined sentence explains why: besides sky observations, the scribes recorded “the market value of barley, dates, wool, and several other commodities.” The final sentence confirms that these entries give historians “an unusually extensive and detailed record of prices,” so choice B is right.

A.why_wrong: The previous sentence mentions “nightly observations of the Moon and planets,” but the underlined sentence is about what else the scribes recorded, not how they observed the sky.

C.why_wrong: The text says the scribes “also recorded” prices, in addition to their observations; it never ranks the two or says what the scribes valued more.

D.recipe: wrong label, strength read as weakness (REL)
D.why_wrong: The following sentence presents the entries as valuable (“an unusually extensive and detailed record”), not as a weakness of the tablets.

items.notes: Area: history (ancient economy). Key B. Function of a supporting detail whose job is set by the first two sentences (the pattern and the exception), as 2.1’s span supports a claim about significance. A describes the neighbor sentence, D gives the right pointer with the wrong label. “Market value” follows the source’s “market exchange values.”

items.passage: Many vascular plants elevate their spores or seeds so that wind can disperse them widely, but peat mosses of the genus Sphagnum, which are nonvascular, cannot grow tall enough to do so. Spores launched ballistically from so near the ground through still air would travel only a few millimeters. Using high-speed video, physicist Dwight Whitaker and biologist Joan Edwards determined how the moss overcomes this limitation: <u>when a spore capsule ruptures, it generates a vortex ring, a rotating loop of air resembling a miniature smoke ring, that carries the spores upward</u>, where turbulent air currents can then transport them many kilometers.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes how the moss’s spore capsules develop before they are ready to rupture.
It identifies the reason that the moss grows close to the ground instead of growing tall.
It elaborates on the earlier claim that spores launched from near the ground through still air travel only a few millimeters.
It explains how the moss lifts its spores high enough for the wind to carry them far.
items.explanation: The text says that Sphagnum “cannot grow tall enough” to hold its spores where wind can disperse them, a “limitation” the researchers found the moss overcomes. The underlined portion gives the answer: a rupturing capsule “generates a vortex ring ... that carries the spores upward,” where “turbulent air currents can then transport them many kilometers.” So the portion explains how the moss lifts its spores high enough to be dispersed, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The portion begins at the moment the capsule “ruptures”; the text says nothing about how capsules develop beforehand.

B.why_wrong: The text treats the moss’s short height as the limitation (“cannot grow tall enough”); the underlined portion describes how the moss overcomes it, not why the moss is short.

C.recipe: wrong relation to the previous sentence (REL)
C.why_wrong: The previous sentence adds to the limitation; the underlined portion does not elaborate on it but explains how the moss avoids it, since the ring carries spores “upward” rather than leaving them a few millimeters away.

Science article record (DOI): author affiliations Dwight L. Whitaker, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Pomona College; Joan Edwards, Biology Department, Williams College (confirms “biologist”)

items.passage: Histories of bacterial genetics usually place Joshua Lederberg, a recipient of the 1958 Nobel Prize, at the center of the field’s founding, yet his wife and collaborator, microbiologist Esther Lederberg, made discoveries that such histories frequently attribute to him or omit entirely. She identified lambda phage, a virus that infects bacteria and later became an essential tool of genetic research, and she helped develop replica plating, a technique for transferring bacterial colonies from one culture dish to numerous others simultaneously. Her standing in the history of microbiology should be as secure as her husband’s.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how Joshua and Esther Lederberg divided the work on the research that earned a Nobel Prize
To describe the techniques that early researchers in bacterial genetics used to study viruses
To argue that Esther Lederberg’s contributions to bacterial genetics deserve more recognition than they usually get
To suggest that the 1958 Nobel Prize should have been awarded to Esther Lederberg instead of her husband
items.explanation: The text says that histories of the field “frequently attribute” Esther Lederberg’s discoveries to her husband “or omit entirely,” then names two of them, lambda phage and replica plating. It ends with an explicit judgment: “Her standing in the history of microbiology should be as secure as her husband’s.” The text therefore argues that her contributions deserve more recognition, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The text calls Esther Lederberg Joshua’s “collaborator” but never explains how they divided any work or which research the prize honored.

B.recipe: scope broadened to the whole field (BROAD)
B.why_wrong: The text describes only two contributions by one scientist, and it does so to support its claim about her recognition, not to survey early techniques.

D.why_wrong: The text asks that her standing be “as secure as her husband’s,” not that she should have received the prize instead of him.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Esther Lederberg: discovered lambda phage, devised the first implementation of replica plating (with Joshua Lederberg); wife of Nobel laureate Joshua Lederberg (1958); textbooks often ignore her work and attribute her accomplishments to her husband

items.notes: Area: history of science. Key C. Explicit evaluative close (“should be as secure as”), as 2.18’s “deserve as much fame”; the argument verb is keyed only because the passage argues. D is the near miss (an argument, but stronger than the text’s). The 1958 prize was shared with Beadle and Tatum; the text says only that Joshua Lederberg was “a recipient.”

The following text is from George Egerton’s 1893 short story “The Spell of the White Elf.” The narrator, traveling by steamer along the Norwegian coast, has struck up an acquaintance with an unconventional fellow passenger, a woman.

We sat and talked, <u>or at least she talked and I listened</u>. I don’t remember what she said; I only know that she was making clear to me most of the things that had puzzled me for a long time,—questions that arise in silent hours, that one speculates over, and to which one finds no answer in text-books. How she knew just the subjects that worked in me I knew not; some subtile intuitive sympathy, I suppose, enabled her to find it out.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It qualifies the narrator’s description of the conversation with the passenger.
It reveals that the narrator was too unwell to take part in the conversation.
It suggests that the narrator resented the passenger for doing most of the talking.
It contrasts the narrator’s memory of the conversation with the passenger’s memory of it.
items.explanation: The narrator first says “We sat and talked,” then immediately corrects that description: “or at least she talked and I listened.” The phrase narrows the earlier statement, showing that the passenger did nearly all the speaking. It therefore qualifies the narrator’s description of the conversation, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The excerpt never mentions the narrator’s health; it shows the narrator listening closely to someone who was “making clear” things that had long puzzled her.

C.why_wrong: The narrator values what the passenger said and credits her with “some subtile intuitive sympathy”; nothing suggests resentment.

D.why_wrong: The narrator says “I don’t remember what she said,” but the text never reports how the passenger remembers the conversation.

items.passage:
The following text is from James D. Corrothers’s 1922 poem “Dream and the Song.”

So oft our hearts, belovèd lute,
In blossomy haunts of song are mute;
So long we pore, ’mid murmurings dull,
O’er loveliness unutterable.
So vain is all our passion strong!
The dream is lovelier than the song.

The rose thought, touched by words, doth turn
Wan ashes. Still, from memory’s urn,
The lingering blossoms tenderly
Refute our wilding minstrelsy.
Alas! we work but beauty’s wrong!
The dream is lovelier than the song.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker recalls a time when singing came easily to him and then explains why he has since given up singing altogether.
The speaker praises the beauty of a rose in bloom and then warns that such blossoms soon wither and turn to ashes.
The speaker recounts a long struggle to put loveliness into words and then vows to keep working until his song is equal to his vision.
The speaker describes long efforts to express beauty in song and then concedes that the song falls short of the dream that inspired it.
items.explanation: Each stanza first describes the effort to put beauty into words: “So long we pore, ’mid murmurings dull, / O’er loveliness unutterable,” and a thought “touched by words, doth turn / Wan ashes.” Each then admits the limit of that effort: “So vain is all our passion strong!” and “Alas! we work but beauty’s wrong!” before the refrain “The dream is lovelier than the song.” The poem thus describes efforts and then concedes that a song falls short of the dream, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The poem never says singing was once easy; it says “our hearts ... are mute” and “So long we pore,” and nothing suggests the speaker has given up.

B.why_wrong: The “rose thought” is an idea that turns to “Wan ashes” when it is “touched by words”; the poem is about failing to capture beauty in song, not about real flowers fading.

C.why_wrong: The poem does describe the struggle, but it ends with resignation, not a vow: “So vain is all our passion strong!” and “The dream is lovelier than the song.”

Poets.org: the poem originally appeared in The Book of American Negro Poetry (1922)

C matches the key’s first move in other words and reverses the second; A invents both; B takes the rose and ashes literally. The following text is from Emma Lazarus’s poem “Echoes,” which appeared in the 1889 collection The Poems of Emma Lazarus.

Late-born and woman-souled I dare not hope,
The freshness of the elder lays [poems], the might
Of manly, modern passion shall alight
Upon my Muse’s lips, nor may I cope
(Who veiled and screened by womanhood must grope)
With the world’s strong-armed warriors and recite
The dangers, wounds, and triumphs of the fight;
Twanging the full-stringed lyre through all its scope.
But if thou ever in some lake-floored cave
O’erbrowed by hard rocks, a wild voice wooed and heard,
Answering at once from heaven and earth and wave,
Lending elf-music to thy harshest word,
Misprize [undervalue] thou not these echoes that belong
To one in love with solitude and song.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker contrasts the freshness of older poetry with the poetry of her own time and then argues that poets today should return to the forms of earlier ages.
The speaker acknowledges kinds of poetry that she feels unable to write and then asks that the poetry she does write be valued on its own terms.
The speaker lists the obstacles that keep her from writing about warfare and then resolves to overcome them by writing about battle anyway.
The speaker recalls hearing a mysterious voice in a cave and then explains how that experience led her to write about nature.
items.explanation: The first eight lines name what the speaker, “Late-born and woman-souled,” feels she cannot attain: “the freshness of the elder lays” and the power to “recite / The dangers, wounds, and triumphs of the fight.” The last six lines turn with “But” and ask that her own poems, likened to echoes, not be undervalued: “Misprize [undervalue] thou not these echoes that belong / To one in love with solitude and song.” The poem thus acknowledges kinds of poetry she feels unable to write and then asks that the poetry she does write be valued, as choice B says.

A.recipe: first part partly true, invented argument (INV)
A.why_wrong: The speaker mentions “the freshness of the elder lays” only to say “I dare not hope” for it in her own work; she never urges other poets to return to older forms, and the poem ends by asking that her own “echoes” not be misprized.

C.why_wrong: The first eight lines do say she cannot “recite / The dangers, wounds, and triumphs of the fight,” but the poem never resolves to write about battle; it turns with “But” to ask that “these echoes,” her own poems, not be misprized.

D.recipe: word hook from the cave image, both moves invented (LIT)
D.why_wrong: The cave belongs to a comparison addressed to “thou” (“if thou ever in some lake-floored cave ... a wild voice wooed and heard”), not to a memory of the speaker’s; it likens her poems to echoes and says nothing about how she came to write about nature.

The following text is from Irving Bacheller’s 1900 novel Eben Holden. The narrator recalls a winter journey to a neighboring town that he made as a young boy, accompanied by Uncle Eb, a hired man who looked after him.

We were awed to silence when we came in sight of Hillsborough, with spires looming far into the sky, as it seemed to me then, and <u>buildings that bullied me with their big bulk</u>, so that I had no heart for the spending of the two shillings Uncle Eb had given me. Such sublimity of proportion I have never seen since; and yet it was all very small indeed.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that the narrator was disappointed by how small the town turned out to be.
It explains why the narrator decided to save his money for a later trip to town.
It conveys how intimidated the narrator felt by the size of the town’s buildings.
It indicates that the narrator was afraid of getting lost in the town’s busy streets.
items.explanation: The narrator and Uncle Eb were “awed to silence” at the sight of Hillsborough, and the underlined portion says the buildings “bullied me with their big bulk,” so much that he “had no heart” for spending his money. The portion shows how intimidated the boy felt by the size of the buildings, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The remark that “it was all very small indeed” is the grown narrator’s view looking back; as a boy he found the buildings overwhelming, not disappointing.

B.why_wrong: He “had no heart for the spending” of his shillings because he was overwhelmed; the text says nothing about saving the money for another trip.

D.why_wrong: The text describes spires and buildings, not streets, and never mentions getting lost.

items.passage:
The following text is from William Hale White’s 1881 novel The Autobiography of Mark Rutherford. The narrator, a former Dissenting minister who now works for a London publisher, has just confided his unhappiness to Theresa, the publisher’s niece.

I was beside myself, and I threw myself on my knees, burying my face in Theresa’s lap and sobbing convulsively. She did not repel me, but she gently passed her fingers through my hair. Oh, the transport of that touch! <u>It was as if water had been poured on a burnt hand, or some miraculous Messiah had soothed the delirium of a fever-stricken sufferer, and replaced his visions of torment with dreams of Paradise.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It emphasizes the relief the narrator feels when Theresa comforts him.
It suggests that the narrator has recently recovered from a serious illness.
It reveals that Theresa is unsure how she should respond to the narrator.
It indicates that the narrator regrets having told Theresa about his troubles.
items.explanation: After the narrator breaks down, Theresa “gently passed her fingers through my hair,” and he exclaims, “Oh, the transport of that touch!” The underlined sentence compares her touch to “water ... poured on a burnt hand” and to a sufferer’s “visions of torment” being replaced “with dreams of Paradise,” stressing the relief her comfort gives him, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The “fever-stricken sufferer” is part of a comparison describing how her touch felt; the text does not say the narrator has been ill.

C.why_wrong: Theresa responds at once and kindly: she “did not repel” him and “gently passed her fingers through” his hair.

D.why_wrong: The narrator calls her touch a “transport” and compares it to relief from pain; nothing suggests he regrets confiding in her.

sources.what: William Hale White (as Mark Rutherford), The Autobiography of Mark Rutherford, Dissenting Minister, edited by his friend Reuben Shapcott (1881), Gutenberg 3269: four consecutive sentences copied exactly

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1881). Key A. Figurative sentence that shows a feeling, as 1.1; B is the literal reading of the image (LIT), C and D reverse details the text states. Published under the pen name Mark Rutherford; the source line uses the author’s real name, as CB does for real-name attributions.

review.note: sensitivity read: the Messiah and Paradise simile is a figure of speech in an 1881 novel, not religious advocacy (CB literary items carry “God” and “Earthly Paradise”); judged suitable

items.passage:
The following text is from Patrick Augustine Sheehan’s 1900 novel My New Curate. The narrator, an Irish priest called Father Dan, is speaking with his bishop.

“Father Dan, you are a bit of a litterateur, I understand. Kilronan is vacant. You’ll have plenty of time for poetizing and dreaming there. What do you say to it?”

I put on a little dignity, and, though my heart was beating with delight, I quietly thanked his Lordship. But, when I had passed beyond the reach of episcopal vision, which is far stretching enough, I spun my hat in the air, and shouted like a schoolboy: “Hurrah!”
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why a character decides to turn down a new position
To portray a character’s joy at an offer and his effort to hide it
To describe a disagreement between a priest and his bishop
To suggest that a character worries that he lacks the skills his new position will require
items.explanation: When the bishop offers him Kilronan, the narrator “put on a little dignity” and “quietly thanked his Lordship,” though his “heart was beating with delight.” Once out of the bishop’s sight, he “spun my hat in the air, and shouted like a schoolboy: ‘Hurrah!’” The text portrays his joy at the offer and how he hides it at first, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The narrator thanks the bishop and then shouts “Hurrah!”; nothing suggests he turns the parish down.

C.why_wrong: The bishop makes an offer and the narrator thanks him; the two never disagree.

D.why_wrong: The bishop mentions the narrator’s taste for “poetizing and dreaming” as a reason the parish suits him; the narrator shows delight, not worry about his skills.

sources.what: Patrick Augustine (Canon) Sheehan, My New Curate (Boston: Marlier, Callanan, 1900), chapter II “A Retrospect,” Gutenberg 20295: the bishop’s speech and the narrator’s next two sentences copied exactly; the narrator Father Dan is appointed parish priest of Kilronan

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1900). Key B. Character’s reaction, as 1.5 and 1.9; the second half of the key (hiding the joy before the bishop) is stated plainly, so the item stays easy. D uses the bishop’s “litterateur” as a hook.

items.passage: Before becoming an artist, Patrick Dougherty earned degrees in English and in hospital administration; only afterward did he return to the University of North Carolina to study art history and sculpture. Since 1982, when his first work appeared in an exhibition, he has constructed more than 300 sculptures and installations from sticks and saplings, young trees with flexible trunks. These works are temporary. Over time, the interwoven branches decompose, and the structures gradually collapse.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a common building material and then explains why many artists working today have begun to use it.
It presents an artist’s view of a style of sculpture and then explains why critics disagree with that view.
It explains how a sculpture is made and then compares that method with the methods of other artists.
It describes how a person came to be an artist and then explains some features of the works he creates.
items.explanation: The first sentence traces how Dougherty came to art: after degrees in English and hospital administration, he went back “to study art history and sculpture.” The rest of the text describes his works: more than 300 sculptures and installations “from sticks and saplings” that “are temporary” because “the interwoven branches decompose.” The text thus describes his path to art and then features of his work, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions sticks and saplings only as Dougherty’s materials; it never discusses other artists or why anyone else uses them.

B.why_wrong: The text gives no view of Dougherty’s about a style of sculpture and mentions no critics.

C.recipe: wholly wrong template with an invented comparison (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text mentions “interwoven branches” but never explains a method step by step or compares it with other artists’ methods.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Patrick Dougherty (artist): American environmental artist known for sculptures and installations built with sticks and saplings; B.A. in English (UNC 1967), M.A. in hospital and health administration (Iowa 1969), later returned to UNC to study art history and sculpture; first work in the 1982 North Carolina Biennial; over 300 works; temporary, as the materials disintegrate

items.notes: Area: humanities (sculpture, environmental art). Key D. Two-move structure as 1.13 and 1.19 (introduce a person, then characteristics of the work); the three distractors are wholly wrong templates, as at easy (7 of 9 easy structure distractors). “Saplings” glossed in the passage.

items.passage: Some painters return to the same subject repeatedly over a long career. <u>The Italian artist Giorgio Morandi, for example, spent decades painting a small collection of ordinary objects—bottles, bowls, boxes, and jars—that he kept in his studio in Bologna.</u> He arranged and rearranged these objects on a tabletop, occasionally painting over their surfaces to eliminate labels and reflections. Concentrating on so few objects allowed him to investigate subtle variations in their placement and in the illumination that fell on them.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It provides an example of the kind of painter described in the previous sentence.
It explains why Morandi preferred painting objects to painting landscapes.
It describes the techniques Morandi used to paint the labels on the bottles in his still lifes.
It suggests that Morandi’s paintings were mostly ignored during his lifetime.
items.explanation: The first sentence says, “Some painters return to the same subject repeatedly over a long career.” The underlined sentence introduces Morandi “for example,” noting that he “spent decades painting a small collection of ordinary objects.” It therefore gives an example of the kind of painter described in the previous sentence, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The text never mentions landscapes or says what Morandi preferred to paint instead.

C.why_wrong: Morandi painted over the objects’ surfaces “to eliminate labels and reflections”; the text does not describe him painting labels.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how Morandi’s paintings were received.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Giorgio Morandi: Italian painter (1890–1964) of muted still lifes, lived and worked in Bologna (studio in Via Fondazza); still lifes made from ordinary studio objects (bottles, bowls, boxes, cups, vases, pitchers, jars) repeatedly arranged and rearranged on a tabletop; sometimes painted their surfaces, removing labels and reflections, to study placement, light, scale

items.notes: Area: humanities (painting). Key A. Example of a general claim, as 1.3 (“One such narrative is ...”); the “for example” signal keeps it easy. C reverses a stated detail; B and D invent.

items.passage: Did Neanderthals make jewelry? <u>A team led by Davorka Radovčić of the Croatian Natural History Museum argues that they did, citing eight white-tailed eagle talons excavated at Krapina, a Neanderthal site in present-day Croatia dated to approximately 130,000 years ago.</u> Several of the talons display cut marks, and all of them exhibit polished or abraded surfaces. According to the researchers, these modifications most likely resulted from mounting the talons together in a necklace or bracelet, long before modern humans arrived in Europe.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes the method that researchers used to determine the age of a site.
It presents a view that the rest of the text goes on to dispute.
It offers a response to the question posed in the first sentence.
It explains why few examples of Neanderthal jewelry have been found.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question: “Did Neanderthals make jewelry?” The underlined sentence answers it, reporting that a team led by Radovčić “argues that they did,” citing eagle talons excavated at Krapina. The rest of the text gives their evidence. So the sentence offers a response to the opening question, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The sentence gives the site’s age (“dated to approximately 130,000 years ago”) but does not explain how that age was determined.

B.why_wrong: The rest of the text supports the researchers’ view with evidence (cut marks, polished areas, how the marks were likely made); nothing disputes it.

D.why_wrong: The text never says how many examples of Neanderthal jewelry exist or why they might be rare.

sources.what: Radovčić, Sršen, Radovčić, Frayer 2015, PLoS ONE 10: e0119802, “Evidence for Neandertal jewelry: modified white-tailed eagle claws at Krapina” (PubMed abstract): eight talons, about 130 kyr; four with cut marks, eight with polishing facets or abrasion; features suggest a jewelry assemblage, from mounting in a necklace or bracelet

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleoanthropology). Key C. Question then answer, as 1.18; option wording varied from the model’s (no defines-a-term or contradicts siblings). “Several” for the source’s four of eight talons; “all of them exhibit polished or abraded surfaces” for “eight show polishing facets and/or abrasion.”

items.passage: Measuring physical activity across entire populations has long been difficult, because large-scale data on how people move in their everyday lives have been scarce. Taking advantage of the motion sensors built into smartphones, computer scientist Tim Althoff and colleagues analyzed step counts from more than 700,000 people in 111 countries. They found that a country’s obesity rate was more closely associated with the gap between its most active and least active residents than with its residents’ average activity. That gap tended to be smaller in cities that were more walkable.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It explains why smartphones count people’s steps more accurately than other devices do.
It describes a study that used a common device to examine how physical activity is related to obesity.
It argues that cities should be redesigned so that their residents will walk more each day.
It compares the walking habits of people who live in cities with the habits of people who live in rural areas.
items.explanation: The text explains that measuring physical activity across entire populations “has long been difficult” and that Althoff and colleagues used “the motion sensors built into smartphones” to study step counts in 111 countries. They found that obesity was “more closely associated with the gap between” the most and least active residents than with average activity. The text thus describes a study that used a common device to examine activity and obesity, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says the researchers used smartphone sensors but never compares their accuracy with that of other devices.

C.why_wrong: The text reports that the activity gap “tended to be smaller” in walkable cities; it does not argue for redesigning cities.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions only cities; rural areas never appear.

sources.what: Althoff, Sosič, Hicks, King, Delp, Leskovec 2017, Nature 547: 336–339, “Large-scale physical activity data reveal worldwide activity inequality” (PubMed abstract): smartphone accelerometry, 717,527 people in 111 countries; activity inequality a better predictor of obesity prevalence than average activity; more walkable cities have lower activity inequality

items.notes: Area: social science (public health). Key B. Study report addressing a difficulty, as 1.15; distractors fail on content a student can check by scanning (INV, STANCE), as at easy. “Step counts” simplifies the source’s accelerometer-measured physical activity, which the study reported as steps.
